entries.78c45b5b6909c7d9baa3559ce34a10f6c64b3387: <div sID="gen16269" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="37" osisID="Isa.37" sID="Isa.37"/> <div eID="gen16269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16270" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16271" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have a further repetition of the story which we had before in the book of Kings concerning Sennacherib. In the foregoing chapter we had him conquering and threatening to conquer. In this chapter we have him falling, and at last fallen, in answer to prayer, and in fulfillment of many of the prophecies which we have met with in the foregoing chapters. Here we have, I. Hezekiah's pious reception of Rabshakeh's impious discourse, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. The gracious message he sent to Isaiah to desire his prayers, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.2-Isa.37.5">ver. 2-5</reference>. III. The encouraging answer which Isaiah sent to him from God, assuring him that God would plead his cause against the king of Assyria, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.6-Isa.37.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. IV. An abusive letter which the king of Assyria sent to Hezekiah, to the same purport with Rabshakeh's speech, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.8-Isa.37.13">ver. 8-13</reference>. V. Hezekiah's humble prayer to God upon the receipt of this letter, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.14-Isa.37.20">ver. 14-20</reference>. VI. The further full answer which God sent him by Isaiah, promising him that his affairs should shortly take a happy turn, that the storm should blow over and every thing should appear bright and serene, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.21-Isa.37.35">ver. 21-35</reference>. VII. The immediate accomplishment of this prophecy in the ruin of his army (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.36">ver. 36</reference>) and the murder of himself, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.37-Isa.37.38">ver. 37, 38</reference>. All this was largely opened, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.1-2Kgs.19.37">2 Kings xix.</reference>
entries.6cb1e55d96613cbc910fb924d03d187fea680d59: <div eID="gen16271" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16270" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Hezekiah's Message to Isaiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen16272" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass, when king Hezekiah heard <hi type="italic">it,</hi> that he rent his clothes, and covered himself with sackcloth, and went into the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">2</hi> And he sent Eliakim, who <hi type="italic">was</hi> over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests covered with sackcloth, unto Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz. <hi type="super">3</hi> And they said unto him, Thus saith Hezekiah, This day <hi type="italic">is</hi> a day of trouble, and of rebuke, and of blasphemy: for the children are come to the birth, and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> not strength to bring forth. <hi type="super">4</hi> It may be the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God will hear the words of Rabshakeh, whom the king of Assyria his master hath sent to reproach the living God, and will reprove the words which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God hath heard: wherefore lift up <hi type="italic">thy</hi> prayer for the remnant that is left. <hi type="super">5</hi> So the servants of king Hezekiah came to <reference osisRef="Isa.6">Isaiah.   6</reference> And Isaiah said unto them, Thus shall ye say unto your master, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Be not afraid of the words that thou hast heard, wherewith the servants of the king of Assyria have blasphemed me. <hi type="super">7</hi> Behold, I will send a blast upon him, and he shall hear a rumour, and return to his own land; and I will cause him to fall by the sword in his own land. <div eID="gen16272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16273" type="x-p"/> We may observe here, 1. That the best way to baffle the malicious designs of our enemies against us is to be driven by them to God and to our duty and so to fetch meat out of the eater. Rabshakeh intended to frighten Hezekiah from the Lord, but it proves that he frightens him to the Lord. The wind, instead of forcing the traveller's coat from him, makes him wrap it the closer about him. The more Rabshakeh reproaches God the more Hezekiah studies to honour him, by rending his clothes for the dishonour done to him and attending in his sanctuary to know his mind. 2. That it well becomes great men to desire the prayers of good men and good ministers. Hezekiah sent messengers, and honourable ones, those of the first rank, to Isaiah, to desire his prayers, remembering how much his prophecies of late had plainly looked towards the events of the present day, in dependence upon which, it is probable, he doubted not but that the issue would be comfortable, yet he would have it to be so in answer to prayer: <hi type="italic">This is a day of trouble,</hi> therefore let it be a day of prayer. 3. When we are most at a plunge we should be most earnest in prayer: Now that the <hi type="italic">children are brought to the birth,</hi> but <hi type="italic">there is not strength to bring forth,</hi> now let prayer come, and help at a dead lift. When pains are most strong let prayers be most lively; and, when we meet with the greatest difficulties, then is a time to stir up not ourselves only, but others also, to take hold on God. Prayer is the midwife of mercy, that helps to bring it forth. 4. It is an encouragement to pray though we have but some hopes of mercy (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">It may be the Lord thy God will hear; who knows but he will return and repent?</hi> The <hi type="italic">it may be</hi> of the prospect of the haven of blessings should quicken us with double diligence to ply the oar of prayer. 5. When there is a remnant left, and but a remnant, it concerns us to lift up a prayer for that remnant, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.4">v. 4</reference>. The prayer that reaches heaven must be lifted up by a strong faith, earnest desires, and a direct intention to the glory of God, all which should be quickened when we come to the last stake. 6. Those that have made God their enemy we have no reason to be afraid of, for they are marked for ruin; and, though they may hiss, they cannot hurt. Rabshakeh has blasphemed God, and therefore let not Hezekiah be afraid of him, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.6">v. 6</reference>. He has made God a party to the cause by his invectives, and therefore judgment will certainly be given against him. God will certainly plead his own cause. 7. Sinners' fears are but prefaces to their falls. He shall <hi type="italic">hear the rumour</hi> of the slaughter of his army, which shall oblige him to retire to his own land, and there he shall be slain, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.7">v. 7</reference>. The terrors that pursue him shall bring him at last to the <hi type="italic">king of terrors,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.18.11">Job xviii. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.18.14">14</reference>. The curses that come upon sinners shall overtake them.
entries.eb84f8f0f9e8b7f48908bb68939c81248acf5c82: <div eID="gen16273" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Prayer of Hezekiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen16274" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> So Rabshakeh returned, and found the king of Assyria warring against Libnah: for he had heard that he was departed from Lachish. <hi type="super">9</hi> And he heard say concerning Tirhakah king of Ethiopia, He is come forth to make war with thee. And when he heard <hi type="italic">it,</hi> he sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying, <hi type="super">10</hi> Thus shall ye speak to Hezekiah king of Judah, saying, Let not thy God, in whom thou trustest, deceive thee, saying, Jerusalem shall not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria. <hi type="super">11</hi> Behold, thou hast heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all lands by destroying them utterly; and shalt thou be delivered? <hi type="super">12</hi> Have the gods of the nations delivered them which my fathers have destroyed, <hi type="italic">as</hi> Gozan, and Haran, and Rezeph, and the children of Eden which <hi type="italic">were</hi> in Telassar? <hi type="super">13</hi> Where <hi type="italic">is</hi> the king of Hamath, and the king of Arphad, and the king of the city of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivah? <hi type="super">14</hi> And Hezekiah received the letter from the hand of the messengers, and read it: and Hezekiah went up unto the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and spread it before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">15</hi> And Hezekiah prayed unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying,   16 <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> of hosts, God of Israel, that dwellest <hi type="italic">between</hi> the cherubims, thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> the God, <hi type="italic">even</hi> thou alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth: thou hast made heaven and earth. <hi type="super">17</hi> Incline thine ear, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , and hear; open thine eyes, O <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and see: and hear all the words of Sennacherib, which hath sent to reproach the living God. <hi type="super">18</hi> Of a truth, <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the kings of Assyria have laid waste all the nations, and their countries, <hi type="super">19</hi> And have cast their gods into the fire: for they <hi type="italic">were</hi> no gods, but the work of men's hands, wood and stone: therefore they have destroyed them. <hi type="super">20</hi> Now therefore, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">even</hi> thou only. <div eID="gen16274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16275" type="x-p"/> We may observe here, 1. That, if God give us inward satisfaction in his promise, this may confirm us in our silently bearing reproaches. God answered Hezekiah, but it does not appear that he, after deliberation, sent any answer to Rabshakeh; but, God having taken the work into his own hands, he quietly left the matter with him. <hi type="italic">So Rabshakeh returned</hi> to the king his master for fresh instructions. 2. Those that delight in war shall have enough of it. Sennacherib, without provocation given to him or warning given by him, went forth to war against Judah; and now with as little ceremony the king of Ethiopia goes forth to war against him, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.9">v. 9</reference>. Those that are quarrelsome may expect to be quarrelled with; and God sometimes checks the rage of his enemies by giving it a powerful diversion. 3. It is bad to talk proudly and profanely, but it is worse to write so, for this argues more deliberation and design, and what is written spreads further, lasts longer, and does the more mischief. Atheism and irreligion, written, will certainly be reckoned for another day. 4. Great successes often harden sinners' hearts in their sinful ways and make them the more daring. Because the kings of Assyria have destroyed all lands (though, in fact, they were but a few that fell within their reach), therefore they doubt not but to destroy God's land; because the gods of the nations were unable to help they conclude the God of Israel is so; because the idolatrous kings of Hamath and Arphad became an easy prey to them therefore they doubt not but to destroy God's land; because the idolatrous kings of Hamath and Arphad became an easy prey to them therefore the religious reforming king of Judah must needs be so too. Thus is this proud man ripened for ruin by the sunshine of prosperity. 5. Liberty of access to the throne of grace, and liberty of speech there, are the unspeakable privilege of the Lord's people at all times, especially in times of distress and danger. Hezekiah took Sennacherib's letter, and spread it before the Lord, not designing to make any complaints against him but those grounded upon his own handwriting. Let the thing speak itself; here it is in black and white: <hi type="italic">Open thy eyes, O Lord! and see.</hi> God allows his praying people to be humbly free with him, to utter all their words, as Jephthah did, before him, to spread the letter, whether of a friend or an enemy, before him, and leave the contents, the concern of it, with him. 6. The great and fundamental principles of our religion, applied by faith and improved in prayer, will be of sovereign use to us in our particular exigencies and distresses, whatever they are; to them therefore we must have recourse, and abide by them; so Hezekiah did here. He encouraged himself with this, that the God of Israel is <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts,</hi> of all hosts, of the hosts of Israel, to animate him, of the hosts of their enemies, to dispirit and restrain them,—that he is God <hi type="italic">alone,</hi> and there is none that can stand in competition with him,—that he is the <hi type="italic">God of all the kingdoms of the earth,</hi> and disposes of them all as he pleases; for he made heaven and earth, and therefore both can do any thing and does every thing. 7. When we are afraid of men that are great destroyers we may with humble boldness appeal to God as the great Saviour. They have indeed destroyed the nations, who had thrown themselves out of the protection of the true God by worshipping false gods, but the Lord, the God alone, is our God, our King, our lawgiver, and he will save us, who is <hi type="italic">the Saviour of those that believe.</hi> 8. We have enough to take hold of, in our wrestling with God by prayer, if we can but plead that his glory is interested in our case, that his name will be profaned if we are run down and glorified if we are relieved. Thence therefore will our most prevailing pleas be drawn: "Do it for thy glory's sake."
entries.496a5c58f383cbb6dfd7933d1486dce8361d1e8d: <div eID="gen16275" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Sennacherib Threatened; Sennacherib Destroyed. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen16276" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> Then Isaiah the son of Amoz sent unto Hezekiah, saying, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, Whereas thou hast prayed to me against Sennacherib king of Assyria: <hi type="super">22</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the word which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath spoken concerning him; The virgin, the daughter of Zion, hath despised thee, <hi type="italic">and</hi> laughed thee to scorn; the daughter of Jerusalem hath shaken her head at thee. <hi type="super">23</hi> Whom hast thou reproached and blasphemed? and against whom hast thou exalted <hi type="italic">thy</hi> voice, and lifted up thine eyes on high? <hi type="italic">even</hi> against the Holy One of Israel. <hi type="super">24</hi> By thy servants hast thou reproached the Lord, and hast said, By the multitude of my chariots am I come up to the height of the mountains, to the sides of Lebanon; and I will cut down the tall cedars thereof, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the choice fir trees thereof: and I will enter into the height of his border, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the forest of his Carmel. <hi type="super">25</hi> I have digged, and drunk water; and with the sole of my feet have I dried up all the rivers of the besieged places. <hi type="super">26</hi> Hast thou not heard long ago, <hi type="italic">how</hi> I have done it; <hi type="italic">and</hi> of ancient times, that I have formed it? now have I brought it to pass, that thou shouldest be to lay waste defenced cities <hi type="italic">into</hi> ruinous heaps. <hi type="super">27</hi> Therefore their inhabitants <hi type="italic">were</hi> of small power, they were dismayed and confounded: they were <hi type="italic">as</hi> the grass of the field, and <hi type="italic">as</hi> the green herb, <hi type="italic">as</hi> the grass on the housetops, and <hi type="italic">as corn</hi> blasted before it be grown up. <hi type="super">28</hi> But I know thy abode, and thy going out, and thy coming in, and thy rage against me. <hi type="super">29</hi> Because thy rage against me, and thy tumult, is come up into mine ears, therefore will I put my hook in thy nose, and my bridle in thy lips, and I will turn thee back by the way by which thou camest. <hi type="super">30</hi> And this <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a sign unto thee, Ye shall eat <hi type="italic">this</hi> year such as groweth of itself; and the second year that which springeth of the same: and in the third year sow ye, and reap, and plant vineyards, and eat the fruit thereof. <hi type="super">31</hi> And the remnant that is escaped of the house of Judah shall again take root downward, and bear fruit upward: <hi type="super">32</hi> For out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant, and they that escape out of mount Zion: the zeal of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts shall do this. <hi type="super">33</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> concerning the king of Assyria, He shall not come into this city, nor shoot an arrow there, nor come before it with shields, nor cast a bank against it. <hi type="super">34</hi> By the way that he came, by the same shall he return, and shall not come into this city, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">35</hi> For I will defend this city to save it for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake. <hi type="super">36</hi> Then the angel of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> went forth, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred and fourscore and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they <hi type="italic">were</hi> all dead corpses. <hi type="super">37</hi> So Sennacherib king of Assyria departed, and went and returned, and dwelt at Nineveh. <hi type="super">38</hi> And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword; and they escaped into the land of Armenia: and Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead. <div eID="gen16276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16277" type="x-p"/> We may here observe, 1. That those who receive messages of terror from men with patience, and send messages of faith to God by prayer, may expect messages of grace and peace from God for their comfort, even when they are most cast down. Isaiah sent a long answer to Hezekiah's prayer in God's name, sent it in writing (for it was too long to be sent by word of mouth), and sent it by way of return to his prayer, relation being thereunto had: "<hi type="italic">Whereas thou hast prayed to me,</hi> know, for thy comfort, that thy prayer is heard." Isaiah might have referred him to the prophecies he had delivered (particularly that <reference osisRef="Isa.10.1-Isa.10.34">ch. x.</reference>) and bid him pick out an answer from thence; but, that he might have abundant consolation, a message is sent him on purpose. The correspondence between earth and heaven is never let fall on God's side. 2. Those who magnify themselves, especially who magnify themselves against God and his people, do really vilify themselves, and made themselves contemptible, in the eyes of all wise men: <hi type="italic">"The virgin, the daughter of Zion, has despised</hi> Sennacherib, and all his impotent malice and menaces; she knows that, while she preserves her integrity, she is sure of the divine protection, and that though the enemy may bark he cannot bite. All his threats are a jest; it is all but <hi type="italic">brutum fulmen—a mere flash,</hi>" 3. Those who abuse the people of God affront God himself; and he takes what is said and done against them as said and done against himself: "<hi type="italic">Whom hast thou reproached?</hi> Even <hi type="italic">the Holy One of Israel,</hi> whom thou hast <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> reproached because he is a Holy One." And it aggravated the indignity Sennacherib did to God that he not only reproached him himself, but set his servants on to do the same: <hi type="italic">By thy servants,</hi> the abjects, <hi type="italic">thou hast reproached me.</hi> 4. Those who boast of themselves and their own achievements reflect upon God and his providence: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast said, I have digged, and drunk water;</hi> I have done mighty feats, and will do more; and wilt not own that <hi type="italic">I have done it,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.37.24-Isa.37.26">v. 24-26</reference>. The most active men are no more than God makes them, and God makes them no more than of old he designed to make them: "<hi type="italic">What I have formed of ancient times,</hi> in an eternal counsel, <hi type="italic">now have I brought to pass</hi>" (for God does all according to the counsel of his will), "<hi type="italic">that thou shouldst be to lay waste defenced cities;</hi> it is therefore intolerable arrogance to make it thy own doing." 5. All the malice, and all the motions and projects, of the church's enemies, are under the cognizance and check of the church's God. Sennacherib was active and quick, here, and there, and every where, but God knew his going out and coming in, and had always an eye upon him, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.28">v. 28</reference>. And that was not all; he had a hand upon him too, a strict hand, a strong hand, <hi type="italic">a hook in his nose and a bridle in his lips,</hi> with which, though he was very headstrong and unruly, he could and would <hi type="italic">turn him back by the way which he came,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.37.29">v. 29</reference>. <hi type="italic">Hitherto he shall come and no further.</hi> God had signed Sennacherib's commission against Judah (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.6">ch. x. 6</reference>); here he supersedes it. He has frightened them, but he must not hurt them, and therefore is discharged from going any further; nay, his commitment is here signed, by which he is clapped up, to answer for what he had done beyond his commission. 6. God is his people's bountiful benefactor, as well as their powerful protector, both a sun and a shield to those that trust in him. Jerusalem shall be defended (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.35">v. 35</reference>), the besiegers shall not come into it, no, nor come before it with any regular attack, but they shall be routed before they begin the siege, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.33">v. 33</reference>. But this is not all; God will return in mercy to his people, and will do them good. Their land shall be more than ordinarily fruitful, so that their losses shall be abundantly repaired; they shall not feel any of the ill effects either of the enemies' wasting the country or of their own being taken off from husbandry. But the earth, as at first, shall bring forth of itself, and they shall live and live plentifully upon its spontaneous productions. The blessing of the Lord can, when he pleases, make rich without the hand of the diligent. And let them not think that the desolations of their country would excuse them from observing the sabbatical year, which happened (as it should seem) the year after, and when they were not to plough or sow; no, though they had not now their usual stock beforehand for that year, yet they must religiously observe it, and depend upon God to provide for them. God must be trusted in the way of duty. 7. There is no standing before the judgments of God when they come with commission. (1.) The greatest numbers cannot stand before them: one angel shall, in one night, lay a vast army of men dead upon the spot, when God commissions him so to do, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.36">v. 36</reference>. Here are 185,000 brave soldiers in an instant turned into so many dead corpses. Many think the <reference osisRef="Ps.76.1-Ps.76.12">76th Psalm</reference> was penned upon occasion of this defeat, where from <hi type="italic">the spoiling of the stout-hearted,</hi> and sending them to sleep their long sleep (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.5">v. 5</reference>), it is inferred that God is <hi type="italic">more glorious and excellent than the mountains of prey</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.4">v. 4</reference>), and that <hi type="italic">he, even he, is to be feared,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.37.7">v. 7</reference>. Angels are employed, more than we are aware of, as ministers of God's justice, to punish the pride and break the power of wicked men. (2.) The greatest men cannot stand before them: <hi type="italic">The great king, the king of Assyria,</hi> looks very little when he is forced to return, not only with shame, because he cannot accomplish what he had projected with so much assurance, but with terror and fear, lest the angel that had destroyed his army should destroy him; yet he is made to look less when his own sons, who should have guarded him, sacrificed him to his idol, whose protection he sought, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.37-Isa.37.38">v. 37, 38</reference>. God can quickly stop their breath who <hi type="italic">breathe out threatenings and slaughter</hi> against his people, and will do it when they have filled up the measure of their iniquity; and <hi type="italic">the Lord is known by</hi> these <hi type="italic">judgments which he executes,</hi> known to be a God that resists the proud. Many prophecies were fulfilled in this providence, which should encourage us, as far as they look further, and are designed as common and general assurances of the safety of the church and of all that trust in God, to depend upon God for the accomplishment of them. He that has delivered does and will deliver. Lord, forgive our enemies; but, <hi type="italic">so let all thy enemies perish, O Lord!</hi>  <chapter eID="Isa.37"/> <div eID="gen16277" type="x-p"/>

Continuation of the Narrative in the Thirty-sixth Chapter.</title> <div sID="gen15111" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8985"/><hi type="bold">1. sackcloth--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.20.2">Is 20:2</reference>).<div eID="gen15111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15112" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">house of the Lord--</hi>the sure resort of God's people in distress (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.16">Psa 73:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.77.13">77:13</reference>). <div eID="gen15112" type="x-p"/>

entries.9b3408e09dcf68534bea85ea9d77c9fe63f0efdb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8987"/><div sID="gen15114" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8987"/><hi type="bold">3. rebuke--</hi>that is, the Lord's rebuke for His people's sins (<reference osisRef="Ps.149.7">Psa 149:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.5.9">Ho 5:9</reference>).<div eID="gen15114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15115" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blasphemy--</hi>blasphemous railing of Rab-shakeh.<div eID="gen15115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15116" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the children, &c.--</hi>a proverbial expression for, We are in the most extreme danger and have no power to avert it (compare <reference osisRef="Hos.13.13">Ho 13:13</reference>). <div eID="gen15116" type="x-p"/>

entries.d91fcc9527a4205b91f884be14450e589b3f8964: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8990"/><div sID="gen15122" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8990"/><hi type="bold">7. blast--</hi>rather, "I will put a spirit (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.6">Is 28:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.23">1Ki 22:23</reference>) into him," that is, so influence his judgment that when he hears the report (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.9">Is 37:9</reference>, concerning Tirhakah), he shall return [Gesenius]; the "report" also of the destruction of his army at Jerusalem, reaching Sennacherib, while he was in the southwest of Palestine on the borders of Egypt, led him to retreat.<div eID="gen15122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15123" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the sword--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.37.38">Is 37:38</reference>). <div eID="gen15123" type="x-p"/>
entries.312f04bc061a58762416cb854ab27fcc3d0fd7af: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8991"/><div sID="gen15124" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8991"/><hi type="bold">8. returned--</hi>to the camp of his master.<div eID="gen15124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15125" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Libnah--</hi>meaning "whiteness," the Blanche-garde of the Crusaders [Stanley]. Eusebius and Jerome place it more south, in the district of Eleutheropolis, ten miles northwest of Lachish, which Sennacherib had captured (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.36.2">Is 36:2</reference>). Libnah was in Judea and given to the priests (<reference osisRef="1Chr.6.54">1Ch 6:54</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.57">57</reference>). <div eID="gen15125" type="x-p"/>
entries.76672745894fd9587a3c8d91cfebe729df720417: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8992"/><div sID="gen15126" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8992"/><hi type="bold">9. Tirhakah--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.17.12">Is 17:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.18.6">Is 18:6</reference>). Egypt was in part governed by three successive Ethiopian monarchs, for forty or fifty years: Sabacho, Sevechus, and Tirhakah. Sevechus retired from Lower Egypt owing to the resistance of the priests, whereupon Sethos, a prince-priest, obtained supreme power with Tanis (Zoan in Scripture), or Memphis, as his capital. The Ethiopians retained Upper Egypt under Tirhakah, with Thebes as the capital. Tirhakah's fame as a conqueror rivalled that of Sesostris; he, and one at least, of the Pharaohs of Lower Egypt, were Hezekiah's allies against Assyria. The tidings of his approach made Sennacherib the more anxious to get possession of Jerusalem before his arrival.<div eID="gen15126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15127" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sent--</hi><reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.9">2Ki 19:9</reference> more fully expresses Sennacherib's eagerness by adding "again." <div eID="gen15127" type="x-p"/>

entries.bdaeb014fa6c2a09faf3ef8eff8ca8473edcc899: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8995"/><div sID="gen15131" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8995"/><hi type="bold">12. Gozan--</hi>in Mesopotamia, on the Chabour (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.6">2Ki 17:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.11">18:11</reference>). Gozan is the name of the district, Chabour of the river.<div eID="gen15131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15132" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Haran--</hi>more to the west. Abraham removed to it from Ur (<reference osisRef="Gen.11.31">Ge 11:31</reference>); the Carroe of the Romans.<div eID="gen15132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15133" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Rezeph--</hi>farther west, in Syria.<div eID="gen15133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15134" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Eden--</hi>There is an ancient village, Adna, north of Baghdad. Some think Eden to be the name of a region (of Mesopotamia or its vicinity) in which was Paradise; Paradise was not Eden itself (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.8">Ge 2:8</reference>). "A garden in Eden."<div eID="gen15134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15135" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Telassar--</hi>now Tel-afer, west of Mosul [Layard]. Tel means a "hill" in Arabic and Assyrian names. <div eID="gen15135" type="x-p"/>

entries.d6f274b726674302d5704b9cb4b6c070a253b400: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8997"/><div sID="gen15137" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8997"/><hi type="bold">14. spread--</hi>unrolled the scroll of writing. entries.0304eea518cf46bac7667966e4b9ada203fe44e6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8998"/><div sID="gen15138" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8998"/><hi type="bold">16. dwellest--</hi>the Shekinah, or fiery symbol of God's presence, dwelling in the temple with His people, is from shachan, "to dwell" (<reference osisRef="Exod.25.22">Ex 25:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.80.1">Psa 80:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.99.1">99:1</reference>).<div eID="gen15138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15139" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cherubim--</hi>derived by transposition from either a Hebrew root, rachab, to "ride"; or rather, barach, to "bless." They were formed out of the same mass of pure gold as the mercy seat itself (<reference osisRef="Exod.25.19">Ex 25:19</reference>, Margin). The phrase, "dwellest between the cherubim," arose from their position at each end of the mercy seat, while the Shekinah, and the awful name, Jehovah, in written letters, were in the intervening space. They are so inseparably associated with the manifestation of God's glory, that whether the Lord is at rest or in motion, they always are mentioned with Him (<reference osisRef="Num.7.89">Nu 7:89</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.10">Psa 18:10</reference>). (1) They are first mentioned (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.24">Ge 3:24</reference>) "on the edge of" (as "on the east" may be translated) Eden; the Hebrew for "placed" is properly to "place in a tabernacle," which implies that this was a local tabernacle in which the symbols of God's presence were manifested suitably to the altered circumstances in which man, after the fall, came before God. It was here that Cain and Abel, and the patriarchs down to the flood, presented their offerings: and it is called "the presence of the Lord" (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.16">Ge 4:16</reference>). When those symbols were removed at the close of that early patriarchal dispensation, small models of them were made for domestic use, called, in Chaldee, "seraphim" or "teraphim." (2) The cherubim, in the Mosaic tabernacle and Solomon's temple, were the same in form as those at the outskirts of Eden: compound figures, combining the distinguishing properties of several creatures: the ox, chief among the tame and useful animals; the lion among the wild ones; the eagle among birds; and man, the head of all (the original headship of man over the animal kingdom, about to be restored in Jesus Christ, <reference osisRef="Ps.8.4-Ps.8.8">Psa 8:4-8</reference>, is also implied in this combination). They are, throughout Scripture, represented as distinct from God; they could not be likenesses of Him which He forbade in any shape. (3) They are introduced in the third or gospel dispensation (<reference osisRef="Rev.4.6">Re 4:6</reference>) as "living creatures" (not so well translated "beasts" in English Version), not angels, but beings closely connected with the redeemed Church. So also in Eze 1:5-25; 10:1-22. Thus, throughout the three dispensations, they seem to be symbols of those who in every age should officially study and proclaim the manifold wisdom of God.<div eID="gen15139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15140" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou alone--</hi>literally, "Thou art He who alone art God of all the kingdoms"; whereas Sennacherib had classed Jehovah with the heathen gods, he asserts the nothingness of the latter and the sole lordship of the former. <div eID="gen15140" type="x-p"/>

entries.fae4a4326a0460f24dd3b29d1275e69d55bdb086: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9000"/><div sID="gen15142" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9000"/><hi type="bold">18. have laid waste--</hi>conceding the truth of the Assyrian's allegation (<reference osisRef="Isa.36.18-Isa.36.20">Is 36:18-20</reference>), but adding the reason, "For they were no gods." <div eID="gen15142" type="x-p"/>
entries.60515e225ad2f13b84fc58e03fd8ce0bb29b4a60: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9001"/><div sID="gen15143" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9001"/><hi type="bold">19. cast ... gods into ... fire--</hi>The policy of the Assyrians in order to alienate the conquered peoples from their own countries was, both to deport them elsewhere, and to destroy the tutelary idols of their nation, the strongest tie which bound them to their native land. The Roman policy was just the reverse. <div eID="gen15143" type="x-p"/>

Whereas thou hast prayed to me--</hi>that is, hast not relied on thy own strength but on Me (compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.20">2Ki 19:20</reference>). "That which thou hast prayed to Me against Sennacherib, I have heard" (<reference osisRef="Ps.65.2">Psa 65:2</reference>). <div eID="gen15145" type="x-p"/>
entries.282fb14cd228f0efb7c1e79e0d3e52e91556615b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9004"/><div sID="gen15146" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9004"/>22. Transition to poetry: in parallelism.<div eID="gen15146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15147" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">virgin ... daughter--</hi>honorable terms. "Virgin" implies that the city is, as yet, inviolate. "Daughter" is an abstract collective feminine personification of the population, the child of the place denoted (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.23.10">Is 23:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.8">Is 1:8</reference>). Zion and her inhabitants.<div eID="gen15147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15148" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shaken ... head--</hi>in scorn (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.7">Psa 22:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.109.25">109:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.27.39">Mt 27:39</reference>). With us to shake the head is a sign of denial or displeasure; but gestures have different meanings in different countries (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.9">Is 58:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.6">Eze 25:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.15">Zep 2:15</reference>). <div eID="gen15148" type="x-p"/>
entries.82dc87336b957ce614308c7d63c6897de5244e31: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9005"/><div sID="gen15149" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9005"/><hi type="bold">23. Whom--</hi>not an idol. <div eID="gen15149" type="x-p"/>
entries.85b3365ff17bb327ecf07fa608bc575de6ac869f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9006"/><div sID="gen15150" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9006"/><hi type="bold">24. said--</hi>virtually. Hast thou within thyself?<div eID="gen15150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15151" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">height--</hi>imagery from the Assyrian felling of trees in Lebanon (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.8">Is 14:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.9">33:9</reference>); figuratively for, "I have carried my victorious army through the regions most difficult of access, to the most remote lands."<div eID="gen15151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15152" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sides--</hi>rather, "recesses" [G. V. Smith].<div eID="gen15152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15153" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fir trees--</hi>not cypresses, as some translate; pine foliage and cedars are still found on the northwest side of Lebanon [Stanley].<div eID="gen15153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15154" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">height of ... border--</hi>In <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.23">2Ki 19:23</reference>, "the lodgings of his borders." Perhaps on the ascent to the top there was a place of repose or caravansary, which bounded the usual attempts of persons to ascend [Barnes]. Here, simply, "its extreme height."<div eID="gen15154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15155" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forest of ... Carmel--</hi>rather, "its thickest forest." "Carmel" expresses thick luxuriance (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.10.18">Is 10:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.17">Is 29:17</reference>). <div eID="gen15155" type="x-p"/>
entries.3f4d6fa12e385900dc060e712ca55626aaed9f2c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9007"/><div sID="gen15156" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9007"/><hi type="bold">25. digged, and drunk water--</hi>In <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.24">2Ki 19:24</reference>, it is "strange waters." I have marched into foreign lands where I had to dig wells for the supply of my armies; even the natural destitution of water there did not impede my march.<div eID="gen15156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15157" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rivers of ... besieged places--</hi>rather, "the streams (artificial canals from the Nile) of Egypt." "With the sole of my foot," expresses that as soon as his vast armies marched into a region, the streams were drunk up by them; or rather, that the rivers proved no obstruction to the onward march of his armies. So <reference osisRef="Isa.19.4-Isa.19.6">Is 19:4-6</reference>, referring to Egypt, "the river--brooks of defense--shall be dried up." Horsley, translates the Hebrew for "besieged places," "rocks." <div eID="gen15157" type="x-p"/>
entries.5da2b545400e418e2c63fd00416b5022c4bfec1a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9008"/><div sID="gen15158" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9008"/>26. Reply of God to Sennacherib.<div eID="gen15158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15159" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">long ago--</hi>join, rather, with "I have done it." Thou dost boast that it is all by thy counsel and might: but it is I who, long ago, have ordered it so (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Is 22:11</reference>); thou wert but the instrument in My hands (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">Is 10:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.15">15</reference>). This was the reason why "the inhabitants were of small power before thee" (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.27">Is 37:27</reference>), namely, that I ordered it so; yet thou art in My hands, and I know thy ways (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.28">Is 37:28</reference>), and I will check thee (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.29">Is 37:29</reference>). Connect also, "I from ancient times have arranged ('formed') it." However, English Version is supported by <reference osisRef="Isa.33.13">Is 33:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.6">45:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.5">48:5</reference>. <div eID="gen15159" type="x-p"/>
entries.343223ffb8a090ad38116fb8c55e4c7af5a019b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9009"/><div sID="gen15160" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9009"/><hi type="bold">27. Therefore--</hi>not because of thy power, but because I made them unable to withstand thee.<div eID="gen15160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grass--</hi>which easily withers (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.6">Is 40:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.2">Psa 37:2</reference>).<div eID="gen15161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15162" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">on ... housetops--</hi>which having little earth to nourish it fades soonest (<reference osisRef="Ps.129.6-Ps.129.8">Psa 129:6-8</reference>).<div eID="gen15162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15163" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">corn blasted before it be grown up--</hi>Smith translates, "The cornfield (frail and tender), before the corn is grown." <div eID="gen15163" type="x-p"/>
entries.b32d997e9fbd9621b26cdb0a97f8b123dbafe0d1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9010"/><div sID="gen15164" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9010"/><hi type="bold">28. abode--</hi>rather, "sitting down" (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.2">Psa 139:2</reference>). The expressions here describe a man's whole course of life (<reference osisRef="Deut.6.7">De 6:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.6">28:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.3.7">1Ki 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.121.8">Psa 121:8</reference>). There is also a special reference to Sennacherib's first being at home, then going forth against Judah and Egypt, and raging against Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.4">Is 37:4</reference>). <div eID="gen15164" type="x-p"/>
entries.5f826b71612c72883637a4c1a2f38e3038bca601: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9011"/><div sID="gen15165" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9011"/><hi type="bold">29. tumult--</hi>insolence.<div eID="gen15165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15166" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hook in ... nose--</hi>Like a wild beast led by a ring through the nose, he shall be forced back to his own country (compare <reference osisRef="Job.41.1">Job 41:1</reference>, 2; <reference osisRef="Ezek.19.4">Eze 19:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.4">29:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.4">38:4</reference>). In a bas-relief of Khorsabad, captives are led before the king by a cord attached to a hook, or ring, passing through the under lip or the upper lip, and nose. <div eID="gen15166" type="x-p"/>
entries.9573525e28dbea375eb2774c1d155fbd2faf0de0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9012"/><div sID="gen15167" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9012"/>30. Addressed to Hezekiah.<div eID="gen15167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15168" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sign--</hi>a token which, when fulfilled, would assure him of the truth of the whole prophecy as to the enemy's overthrow. The two years, in which they were sustained by the spontaneous growth of the earth, were the two in which Judea had been already ravaged by Sennacherib (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.10">Is 32:10</reference>). Thus translate: "Ye did eat (the first year) such as groweth of itself, and in the second year that ... but in this third year sow ye," &c., for in this year the land shall be delivered from the foe. The fact that Sennacherib moved his camp away immediately after shows that the first two years refer to the past, not to the future [Rosenmuller]. Others, referring the first two years to the future, get over the difficulty of Sennacherib's speedy departure, by supposing that year to have been the sabbatical year, and the second year the jubilee; no indication of this appears in the context. <div eID="gen15168" type="x-p"/>
entries.ad04a8da6eafd76c4740b5b85ffe260515d1d630: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9013"/><div sID="gen15169" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9013"/><hi type="bold">31. remnant--</hi>Judah remained after the ten tribes were carried away; also those of Judah who should survive Sennacherib's invasion are meant. <div eID="gen15169" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e2c31ff02b35e722fecdd2046741d77ffcbb836: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9014"/><div sID="gen15170" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9014"/><hi type="bold">33. with shields--</hi>He did come near it, but was not allowed to conduct a proper siege.<div eID="gen15170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15171" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bank--</hi>a mound to defend the assailants in attacking the walls. <div eID="gen15171" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5a54a96fcbd1876c0dbcce28789d242c7ce5625: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9015"/><div sID="gen15172" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9015"/>34. (See <reference osisRef="Isa.37.29">Is 37:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.37">37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.5-Isa.29.8">Is 29:5-8</reference>). <div eID="gen15172" type="x-p"/>
entries.dcbb9c487b8a76b7cd76f5efb8183b04bf8d1ddc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9016"/><div sID="gen15173" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9016"/><hi type="bold">35. I will defend--</hi>Notwithstanding Hezekiah's measures of defense (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.3-2Chr.32.5">2Ch 32:3-5</reference>), Jehovah was its true defender.<div eID="gen15173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15174" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mine own sake--</hi>since Jehovah's name was blasphemed by Sennacherib (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.23">Is 37:23</reference>).<div eID="gen15174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15175" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">David's sake--</hi>on account of His promise to David (<reference osisRef="Ps.132.17">Psa 132:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.18">18</reference>), and to Messiah, the heir of David's throne (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.7">Is 9:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">11:1</reference>). <div eID="gen15175" type="x-p"/>
entries.d93c1e730333242746e870924697ce5164e3a24d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9017"/><div sID="gen15176" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9017"/>36. Some attribute the destruction to the agency of the plague (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.33.24">Is 33:24</reference>), which may have caused Hezekiah's sickness, narrated immediately after; but <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Is 33:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.4">4</reference>, proves that the Jews spoiled the corpses, which they would not have dared to do, had there been on them infection of a plague. The secondary agency seems, from <reference osisRef="Isa.29.6">Is 29:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.30">30:30</reference>, to have been a storm of hail, thunder, and lightning (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.9.22-Exod.9.25">Ex 9:22-25</reference>). The simoon belongs rather to Africa and Arabia than Palestine, and ordinarily could not produce such a destructive effect. Some few of the army, as <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.21">2Ch 32:21</reference> seems to imply, survived and accompanied Sennacherib home. Herodotus (2.141) gives an account confirming Scripture in so far as the sudden discomfiture of the Assyrian army is concerned. The Egyptian priests told him that Sennacherib was forced to retreat from Pelusium owing to a multitude of field mice, sent by one of their gods, having gnawed the Assyrians' bow-strings and shield-straps. Compare the language (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.33">Is 37:33</reference>), "He shall not shoot an arrow there, nor come before it with shields," which the Egyptians corrupted into their version of the story. Sennacherib was as the time with a part of his army, not at Jerusalem, but on the Egyptian frontier, southwest of Palestine. The sudden destruction of the host near Jerusalem, a considerable part of his whole army, as well as the advance of the Ethiopian Tirhakah, induced him to retreat, which the Egyptians accounted for in a way honoring to their own gods. The mouse was the Egyptian emblem of destruction. The Greek Apollo was called Sminthian, from a Cretan word for "a mouse," as a tutelary god of agriculture, he was represented with one foot upon a mouse, since field mice hurt corn. The Assyrian inscriptions, of course, suppress their own defeat, but nowhere boast of having taken Jerusalem; and the only reason to be given for Sennacherib not having, amidst his many subsequent expeditions recorded in the monuments, returned to Judah, is the terrible calamity he had sustained there, which convinced him that Hezekiah was under the divine protection. Rawlinson says, In Sennacherib's account of his wars with Hezekiah, inscribed with cuneiform characters in the hall of the palace of Koyunjik, built by him (a hundred forty feet long by a hundred twenty broad), wherein even the Jewish physiognomy of the captives is portrayed, there occurs a remarkable passage; after his mentioning his taking two hundred thousand captive Jews, he adds, "Then I prayed unto God"; the only instance of an inscription wherein the name of God occurs without a heathen adjunct. The forty-sixth Psalm probably commemorates Judah's deliverance. It occurred in one "night," according to <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.35">2Ki 19:35</reference>, with which Isaiah's words, "when they arose early in the morning," &c., are in undesigned coincidence.<div eID="gen15176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15177" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they ... they--</hi>"the Jews ... the Assyrians." <div eID="gen15177" type="x-p"/>
entries.27093204ca378c6bf959156fd30690bc68e47d21: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9018"/><div sID="gen15178" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9018"/><hi type="bold">37. dwelt at Nineveh--</hi>for about twenty years after his disaster, according to the inscriptions. The word, "dwelt," is consistent with any indefinite length of time. "Nineveh," so called from Ninus, that is, Nimrod, its founder; his name means "exceedingly impious rebel"; he subverted the existing patriarchal order of society, by setting up a system of chieftainship, founded on conquest; the hunting field was his training school for war; he was of the race of Ham, and transgressed the limits marked by God (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.8-Gen.11.25">Ge 10:8-11, 25</reference>), encroaching on Shem's portion; he abandoned Babel for a time, after the miraculous confusion of tongues and went and founded Nineveh; he was, after death, worshipped as Orion, the constellation (see on <reference osisRef="Job.9.9">Job 9:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.38.31">Job 38:31</reference>). <div eID="gen15178" type="x-p"/>
entries.9be9dc8dc3ebdf3337b9bd01c9a9a5e57b2bb30f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9019"/><div sID="gen15179" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9019"/><hi type="bold">38. Nisroch--</hi>Nisr, in Semitic, means "eagle;" the termination och, means "great." The eagle-headed human figure in Assyrian sculptures is no doubt Nisroch, the same as Asshur, the chief Assyrian god; the corresponding goddess was Asheera, or Astarte; this means a "grove," or sacred tree, often found as the symbol of the heavenly hosts (Saba) in the sculptures, as Asshur the Eponymus hero of Assyria (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.11">Ge 10:11</reference>) answered to the sun or Baal, Belus, the title of office, "Lord." This explains "image of the grove" (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.7">2Ki 21:7</reference>). The eagle was worshipper by the ancient Persians and Arabs.<div eID="gen15179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15180" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Esar-haddon--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.2">Ezr 4:2</reference> he is mentioned as having brought colonists into Samaria. He is also thought to have been the king who carried Manasseh captive to Babylon (<reference osisRef="2Chr.33.11">2Ch 33:11</reference>). He built the palace on the mound Nebbiyunus, and that called the southwest palace of Nimroud. The latter was destroyed by fire, but his name and wars are recorded on the great bulls taken from the building. He obtained his building materials from the northwest palaces of the ancient dynasty, ending in Pul. <chapter eID="Isa.37"/>

entries.03b61db3659bd5b6bd9d2d918d97c15adf494a59: <div eID="gen27991" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen27992" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27993" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27993" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27992" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27994" type="x-p"/> Hezekiah is greatly distressed, and sends to Isaiah the prophet to pray for him, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.1-Isa.37.4">Isa 37:1-4</reference>. Isaiah returns a comfortable answer, and predicts the destruction of the king of Assyria and his army, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.5-Isa.37.7">Isa 37:5-7</reference>. Sennacherib, hearing that his kingdom was invaded by the Ethiopians, sends a terrible letter to Hezekiah, to induce him to surrender, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.9-Isa.37.13">Isa 37:9-13</reference>. Hezekiah goes to the temple, spreads the letter before the Lord, and makes a most affecting prayer, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.14-Isa.37.20">Isa 37:14-20</reference>. Isaiah is sent to him to assure him that his prayer is heard; that Jerusalem shall be delivered; and that the Assyrians shall be destroyed, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.21-Isa.37.35">Isa 37:21-35</reference>. That very night a messenger of God slays one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.36">Isa 37:36</reference>. Sennacherib returns to Nineveh, and is slain by his own sons, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.37">Isa 37:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.38">Isa 37:38</reference>.
entries.aae6a74cdb8d5316d42c5314615bb207c684be0f: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen27994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27995" type="x-p"/> Thus shall ye say - כה תאמרון ko tomerun, "thus shall ye (explicitly, earnestly, and positively) say. "The paragogic nun deepens and increases the sense.
entries.d7ecd09d27323fa9ef2c8d2b4b94b76c801bd755: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen27995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27996" type="x-p"/> I will send a blast "I will infuse a spirit into him" - "נותין בו רוח nothen bo roach never signifies any thing but putting a spirit into a person: this was πνευμα δειλιας, the spirit of deceit." - Secker. "I will send a blast" - I do not think that Archbishop Secker has hit the true meaning of these words. I believe רוח ruach means here a pestilential wind, such as the Arabs call simoom, that instantly suffocates both man and beast; and is what is termed "the angel of the Lord," God's messenger of death to the Assyrians, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.36">Isa 37:36</reference>.
entries.608a6cfc88f6a7171c4fe1efedadb3b4e9b9b851: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen27996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27997" type="x-p"/> Rabshakeh returned - From <reference osisRef="Isa.36.2">Isa 36:2</reference>, we learn that the king of Assyria had sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem; now it is likely that Rabshakeh had besieged that place, and that the king of Assyria had taken his station before this city, and dispatched Rabshakeh against Jerusalem. But, as in the verse above it is said, "he had departed from Lachish," probably he had been obliged to raise the siege, and sat down before Libnah, which promised an easier conquest.
entries.7432baa92c56515d02e479d0914b24b8c4b762cd: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen27997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27998" type="x-p"/> He heard say concerning Tirhakah king of Ethiopia - When he heard that Tirhakah king of Ethiopia had come out against him, then he sent that blasphemous manifesto which is contained in <reference osisRef="Isa.37.10-Isa.37.13">Isa 37:10-13</reference>, to terrify Hezekiah into submission. How much was this like, in words and spirit, to the manifesto sent to the Parisians by the late Duke of Brunswick, from the plains of Champaigne, in 1792, which was the forerunner of the mighty torrents of human blood which was shed in the French revolution! And what a blast of God fell upon him and his army - nearly like that which fell on the army of Sennacherib! <div eID="gen27998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27999" type="x-p"/> He sent messengers "He sent messengers again" - The word וישמע vaiyishma, "and he heard, "which occurs the second time in this verse, is repeated by mistake from the beginning of the verse. It is omitted in an ancient MS. It is a mere tautology, and embarrasses the sense. The true reading instead of it is, וישב veyesheb, "and he returned, "which the Septuagint read in this place, απεστρεψε, and which is preserved in the other copy, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.9">2Kgs 19:9</reference> : "He returned and sent, "that is, according to the Hebrew idiom, "he sent again."
entries.661e9b82008c4cd4f26300413981ad8fc58336b1: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen27999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28000" type="x-p"/> As Gozan, and Haran - חרן Charan: but הרן Haran is the reading of four of Kennicott's MSS. and one of De Rossi's.
entries.2b6dba9d3ed0222f58e173285bef16f01c29227a: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen28000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28001" type="x-p"/> And read it "And read them" - ויקראם vayikraem. So MS. Bodl. in this place; and so the other copy; instead of ויקראהו vaiyikraehu, "and read It." <div eID="gen28001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28002" type="x-p"/> And spread it "And spread them" - ויפרשהו vaiyiphresehu. הו hu is upon a rasure in a MS., which probably was at first ם mem. The same mistake as in the foregoing note.
entries.943712366dac8ffa5d9c50ef897bdc53d386e786: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen28002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28003" type="x-p"/> Unto the Lord "Before Jehovah" - That is, in the sanctuary. For אל el, the Syriac, Chaldee, and the other copy, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.15">2Kgs 19:15</reference>, read לפני liphney, "before the face."
entries.4eebc90781947675ee61981518caa5f3e8681576: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen28003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28004" type="x-p"/> The nations - הארצות haratsoth, "the lands; "instead of this word, which destroys the sense, ten of Kennicott's and five of De Rossi's MSS. (one ancient) have here גוים goyim, "nations;" which is undoubtedly the true reading, being preserved also in the other copy; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.17">2Kgs 19:17</reference>. Another MS. suggests another method of rectifying the sense in this place, by reading מלכם malcam, "their king, "instead of ארצם artsam, "their land;" but it ought to be מלכיהם malcheyhem, "all the countries and their kings."
entries.80227e510d6ca1774204fdbef7f9f8a036050fda: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen28004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28005" type="x-p"/> Save us "Save us, we beseech thee" - The supplicating particle, נא na, is supplied here from eighteen MSS., three ancient, of Dr. Kennicott, and ten of De Rossi, and from the other copy; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.19">2Kgs 19:19</reference>. <div eID="gen28005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28006" type="x-p"/> That thou art the Lord, even thou only "That thou Jehovah art the only God" - The word אלהים Elohim, "God, "is lost here in the Hebrew text, but preserved in the other copy; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.19">2Kgs 19:19</reference>. The Syriac and Septuagint seem here to have had in their copies אלהים Elohim, instead of יהוה Yehovah.
entries.b5599f6e6caa1990c225c2064a3023a919526df0: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen28006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28007" type="x-p"/> Then Isaiah - sent unto Hezekiah - The Syriac and Septuagint understand and render the verb passively, was sent. <div eID="gen28007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28008" type="x-p"/> Whereas thou hast prayed to me against Sennacherib "Thy prayer unto me concerning Sennacherib - I have heard" - שמעתי shamati; this word, necessary to the sense, is lost in this place out of the Hebrew text. One MS. of Dr. Kennicott's and one of De Rossi's have it written above the line in a later hand. The Septuagint and Syriac found it in their copies; and it is preserved in the other copy; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.20">2Kgs 19:20</reference>.
entries.56ce2dc4d601d029901166c1f792b14164b14491: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen28008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28009" type="x-p"/> Against the Holy One of Israel - For אל el, to, the other copy has על al, against, rather more properly.
entries.3a5b9338d030832c89741da814bd51cdfa67b381: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen28009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28010" type="x-p"/> By thy servants "By thy messengers" - The text has עבדיך abdeycha, thy servants; but the true reading seems to be מלאכיך malacheycha, thy messengers, as in the other copy, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.23">2Kgs 19:23</reference>; and as the Septuagint and Syriac found it in their copies in this place. <div eID="gen28010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28011" type="x-p"/> Reproached the Lord - אדני Adonai: but one of my MSS. has יהוה אדני Yehovah Adonai, Jehovah the Lord. This reading is not found, I think, in any other MS., but several have יהוה Yehovah for אדני Adonai. <div eID="gen28011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28012" type="x-p"/> I will enter into the height of his border "I will penetrate into his extreme retreats" - The text has מרום marom, the height which seems to have been taken by mistake from the line but one above. Two MSS. have here מלון malon, the lodge or retreat; which is the word in the other copy, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.23">2Kgs 19:23</reference>, and I think is the true reading. <div eID="gen28012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28013" type="x-p"/> The forest of has Carmel - The forest and his fruitful field; that is, I will possess myself of the whole country.
entries.40b472c039759426170bf295e2db4039eb0e4dca: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen28013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28014" type="x-p"/> Water "Strange waters" - The word זרים zarim, strange, lost out of the Hebrew text in this place, is supplied from the other copy. A MS. supplies the word רבים rabbim, many, instead of it. <div eID="gen28014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28015" type="x-p"/> With the sole of my feet - With my infantry. <div eID="gen28015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28016" type="x-p"/> All the rivers of the besieged places "All the canals of fenced places" - The principal cities of Egypt, the scene of his late exploits, were chiefly defended by deep moats, canals, or large lakes, made by labor and art, with which they were surrounded. See Harmer's Observ. 2 p. 304. Claudian introduces Alaric boasting of his conquests in the same extravagant manner: - "Subsidere nostris <div eID="gen28016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28017" type="x-p"/> Sub pedibus montes; arescere vidimus amnes. - <div eID="gen28017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28018" type="x-p"/> Fregi Alpes, galeisque Padum victricibus hausi." <div eID="gen28018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28019" type="x-p"/> De Bello Getic. 526. "The mountains have passed away under our feet; we have seen the rivers dried up. I have broken the Alps, and laden out the Po with our victorious helmets."
entries.3ec5ee9092aaca80ce41305fea8b20dc68993fb9: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen28019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28020" type="x-p"/> Lay waste defended cities into ruinous heaps "Lay waste warlike nations; strong fenced cities" - גלים נצים gallim nitstsim. It is not easy to give a satisfactory account of these two words, which have greatly embarrassed all the interpreters, ancient and modern. For גלים gallim I read גוים goyim, as the Septuagint do in this place, εθνη. The word נצים netsim the Vulgate renders in this place compugnantium; in the parallel place, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.25">2Kgs 19:25</reference>, pugnantium; and the Septuagint μαχιμων, fighting, warlike. This rendering is as well authorized as any other that I know of; and, with the reading of the Septuagint, perfectly clears up the construction. See the margin on all the preceding verses.
entries.a4a668a8818dd4a25b67cd6dcadaf63b884b08c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen28020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28021" type="x-p"/> Corn blasted - שדמה shedemah, parched: it does not appear that there is any good authority for this word. The true reading seems to be שדפה shedephah, blasted, as it is in six MSS. (two ancient) here, and in the other copy.
entries.1f3f2d6983cb772983869efbb193f6a106da52ab: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen28021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28022" type="x-p"/> Will I put my hook in thy nose - Et fraenum meum: Jonathan vocem מתג metheg, interpretatus est זמם zemam, i.e., annulum, sive uncum, eumque ferreum, quem infigunt naribus camelae: eoque trahitur, quoniam illa feris motibus agitur: et hoc est, quod discimus in Talmude; et camela cum annulo narium: scilicet, egreditur die sabbathi. "And my bridle: Jonathan interprets the word metheg by zemam, a ring, or that iron hook which they put in the nostrils of a camel to lead her about, check her in her restiveness, etc. And this is what we mean in the Talmud, when we say, And the camel with the ring of her nostrils shall go out on the Sabbath day." - Jarchi in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.28">2Kgs 19:28</reference>. Ponam circulum in naribus tuis. "I will put a ring in thy nostrils." - Jerome. Just as at this day they put a ring into the nose of the bear, the buffalo, and other wild beasts, to lead them, and to govern them when they are unruly. Bulls are often ringed thus in several parts of England. The Hindoos compare a person who is the slave of his wife to a cow led by the ring in her nose.
entries.a3d323c1c4b8478540039d0c7d08fd70cbff99ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen28022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28023" type="x-p"/> Then the angel - Before "the angel, "the other copy, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.35">2Kgs 19:35</reference>, adds "it came to pass the same night, that " - The Prophet Hosea, <reference osisRef="Hos.1.7">Hos 1:7</reference>, has given a plain prediction of the miraculous deliverance of the kingdom of Judah: - "And to the house of Judah I will be tenderly merciful: <div eID="gen28023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28024" type="x-p"/> And I will save them by Jehovah their God. <div eID="gen28024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28025" type="x-p"/> And I will not save them by the bow; <div eID="gen28025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28026" type="x-p"/> Nor by sword, nor by battle; <div eID="gen28026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28027" type="x-p"/> By horses, nor by horsemen." - L.
entries.c9d21dddc09794aac213d685a858b36d4081b21d: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen28027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28028" type="x-p"/> His sons smote him - What an awful punishment of his blasphemy! Who can harden his neck against God, and be successful? God does not lightly pass by blasphemy against himself, his government, his word, his Son, or his people. Let the profligate take care!  <chapter eID="Isa.37"/> <div eID="gen28028" type="x-p"/>

entries.a138a1d4b2f2a82a92bf2fa5d8adc31b3f29b466: <reference osisRef="Isa.37.1-Isa.37.4">Isa 37:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen13259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13260" type="x-p"/> The king and the deputation apply to Isaiah. <hi type="italic">“And it came to pass, when king Hizkiyahu had heard, he rent his clothes, and wrapped himself in mourning linen, and went into the house of Jehovah. And sent Eliakim the house-minister, and Shebna </hi>(K. omits את)<hi type="italic">the chancellor, and the eldest of the priests, wrapped in mourning linen, to Isaiah son of Amoz, the prophet </hi>(K. <hi type="italic">has what is inadmissible: the prophet son of Amoz</hi>).<hi type="italic">And they said to him, Thus saith Hizkiyahu, A day of affliction, and punishment, and blasphemy is this day; for children are come to the matrix, and there is no strength to bring them forth. Perhaps Jehovah thy God will hear the words </hi>(K. <hi type="italic">all the words</hi>)<hi type="italic">of Rabshakeh, with which the king of Asshur his lord has sent him to revile the living God; and Jehovah thy God will punish for the words which He hath heard, and thou wilt make intercession for the remnant that still exists.”</hi> The distinguished embassy is a proof of the distinction of the prophet himself (Knobel). The character of the deputation accorded with its object, which was to obtain a consolatory word for the king and people. In the form of the instructions we recognise again the flowing style of Isaiah. תּוכחה, as a synonym of מוּסר, נקם, is used as in Hos 5:9; נאצה (from the <hi type="italic">kal</hi> נאץ) according to <reference osisRef="Isa.1.4">Isa 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.24">Isa 5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.52.5">Isa 52:5</reference>, like נאצה (from the <hi type="italic">piel</hi> נאץ), <reference osisRef="Neh.9.18">Neh 9:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.26">Neh 9:26</reference> (reviling, i.e., reviling of God, or blasphemy). The figure of there not being sufficient strength to bring forth the child, is the same as in Isa 66:9. משׁבּר (from שׁבר, syn. פּרץ, <reference osisRef="Gen.38.29">Gen 38:29</reference>) does not signify the actual birth (Luzzatto, <hi type="italic">punto di dover nascere</hi>), nor the delivering-stool (Targum), like <hi type="italic">mashbēr</hi> <hi type="italic">shel</hi>-<hi type="italic">chayyâh</hi>, the delivering-stool of the midwife (<hi type="italic">Kelim</hi> xxiii. 4); but as the subject is the children, and not the mother, the matrix or mouth of the womb, as in Hos 13:13, “He (Ephraim) is an unwise child; when it is time does he not stop in the children’s passage” (<hi type="italic">mashbēr</hi> <hi type="italic">bânı̄m</hi>), i.e., the point which a child must pass, not only with its head, but also with its shoulders and its whole body, for which the force of the pains is often not sufficient? The existing condition of the state resembled such unpromising birth-pains, which threatened both the mother and the fruit of the womb with death, because the matrix would not open to give birth to the child. לדה like דּעה in Isa 11:9. The timid inquiry, which hardly dared to hope, commences with <hi type="italic">'ūlai</hi>. The following future is continued in perfects, the force of which is determined by it: “and He (namely Jehovah, the Targum and Syriac) will punish for the words,” or, as we point it, “there will punish for the words which He hath heard, Jehovah thy God (<hi type="italic">hōkhı̄ach</hi>, referring to a judicial decision, as in a general sense in <reference osisRef="Isa.2.4">Isa 2:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Isa 11:4</reference>); and thou wilt lift up prayer” (i.e., begin to offer it, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.4">Isa 14:4</reference>). “He will hear,” namely as judge and deliverer; “He hath heard,” namely as the omnipresent One. The expression, “to revile the living God” (<hi type="italic">lechârēph 'Elōhı̄m chai</hi>), sounds like a comparison of Rabshakeh to Goliath (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.26">1Sa 17:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.36">1Sa 17:36</reference>). The “existing remnant” was Jerusalem, which was not yet in the enemy’s hand (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.1.8-Isa.1.9">Isa 1:8-9</reference>). The deliverance of the remnant is a key-note of Isaiah’s prophecies. But the prophecy would not be fulfilled, until the grace which fulfilled it had been met by repentance and faith. Hence Hezekiah’s weak faith sues for the intercession of the prophet, whose personal relation to God is here set forth as a closer one than that of the king and priests.
entries.292a956614ed1f3c966feacbf175aca1dbeb918f: <reference osisRef="Isa.37.5-Isa.37.7">Isa 37:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen13260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13261" type="x-p"/> Isaiah’s reply. <hi type="italic">“And the servants of king Hizkiyahu came to Isaiah. And Isaiah said to them </hi>(אליהם, K. להם),<hi type="italic">Speak thus to your lord, Thus saith Jehovah, Be not afraid of the words which thou hast heard, with which the servants of the king of Asshur have blasphemed me! Behold, I will bring a spirit upon him, and he will hear a hearsay, and return to his land; and I cut him down with the sword in his own land.”</hi> Luzzatto, without any necessity, takes ויּאמרוּ in <reference osisRef="Isa.37.3">Isa 37:3</reference> in the modal sense of what they were to do (<hi type="italic">e dovevano dirgli</hi>): they were to say this to him, but he anticipated them at once with the instructions given here. The fact, so far as the style is concerned, is rather this, that <reference osisRef="Isa.37.5">Isa 37:5</reference>, while pointing back, gives the ground for <reference osisRef="Isa.37.6">Isa 37:6</reference> : “and when they had come to him (saying this), he said to them.” נערי we render “servants” (Knappen)<note placement="foot">Knappe is the same word as “<hi type="italic">Knave;</hi>” but we have no word in use now which is an exact equivalent, and knave has entirely lost its original sense of <hi type="italic">servant</hi>. - Tr.</note> after <reference osisRef="Esth.2.2">Est 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.6.3">Est 6:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Esth.6.5">Est 6:5</reference>; it is a more contemptuous expression than עבדי. The <hi type="italic">rūăch</hi> mentioned here as sent by God is a superior force of a spiritual kind, which influences both thought and conduct, as in such other connections as <reference osisRef="Isa.19.14">Isa 19:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.6">Isa 28:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.10">Isa 29:10</reference> (<hi type="italic">Psychol.</hi> p. 295, Anm.). <div eID="gen13261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13262" type="x-p"/> The external occasion which determined the return of Sennacherib, as described in <reference osisRef="Isa.37.36-Isa.37.37">Isa 37:36-37</reference>, was the fearful mortality that had taken place in his army. The <hi type="italic">shemū‛âh</hi> (rumour, hearsay), however, was not the tidings of this catastrophe, but, as the continuation of the account in <reference osisRef="Isa.37.8">Isa 37:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.9">Isa 37:9</reference>, clearly shows, the report of the advance of Tirhakah, which compelled Sennacherib to leave Palestine in consequence of this catastrophe. The prediction of his death is sufficiently special to be regarded by modern commentators, who will admit nothing but the most misty figures as prophecies, as a <hi type="italic">vaticinium post eventum</hi>. At the same time, the prediction of the event which would drive the Assyrian out of the land is intentionally couched in these general terms. The faith of the king, and of the inquirers generally, still needed to be tested and exercised. The time had not yet come for him to be rewarded by a clearer and fuller announcement of the judgment.
entries.630ffca77b5b93b9e70f31a6ea23f797db3a3dd7: <reference osisRef="Isa.37.8-Isa.37.9">Isa 37:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen13262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13263" type="x-p"/> Rabshakeh, who is mentioned alone in both texts as the leading person engaged, returns to Sennacherib, who is induced to make a second attempt to obtain possession of Jerusalem, as a position of great strength and decisive importance. <hi type="italic">“Rabshakeh thereupon returned, and found the king of Asshur warring against Libnah: for he had heard that he had withdrawn from Lachish. And he heard say concerning Tirhakah king of Ethiopia, </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">Behold</hi>)<hi type="italic">, he has come out to make war with thee; and heard, and sent </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">and repeated, and sent</hi>)<hi type="italic">messengers to Hizkiyahu, saying.”</hi> Tirhakah was cursorily referred to in <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1">Isa 18:1</reference>-7. The twenty-fifth dynasty of Manetho contained three Ethiopian rulers: <hi type="italic">Sabakon</hi>, <hi type="italic">Sebichōs</hi> (סוא = סוא), although, so far as we know, the Egyptian names begin with <hi type="italic">Sh</hi>), and <hi type="italic">Tarakos</hi> (<hi type="italic">Tarkos</hi>), Egypt. <hi type="italic">Taharka</hi>, or Heb. with the tone upon the penultimate, <hi type="italic">Tirhâqâh</hi>. The only one mentioned by Herodotus is Sabakon, to whom he attributes a reign of fifty years (ii. 139), i.e., as much as the whole three amount to, when taken in a round sum. If Sebichos is the biblical <hi type="italic">So'</hi>, to whom the lists attribute from twelve to fourteen years, it is perfectly conceivable that Tirhakah may have been reigning in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah.
