But if this took place, as Manetho affirms, 366 years before the conquest of Egypt by Alexander, i.e., from 696 onwards (and the <hi type="italic">Apis-stele</hi>, No. 2037, as deciphered by Vic. de Rougé, <hi type="italic">Revue archéol.</hi> 1863, confirms it), it would be more easily reconcilable with the Assyrian chronology, which represents Sennacherib as reigning from 702-680 (Oppert and Rawlinson), than with the current biblical chronology, according to which Hezekiah’s fourteenth year is certainly not much later than the year 714.<note placement="foot">On the still prevailing uncertainty with regard to the synchronism, see Keil on Kings; and Duncker, <hi type="italic">Geschichte des Alterthums</hi>. pp. 713-4.</note> <div eID="gen13263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13264" type="x-p"/> It is worthy of remark also, that Tirhakah is not described as Pharaoh here, but as the king of Ethiopia (<hi type="italic">melekh</hi> <hi type="italic">Kūsh</hi>; see at <reference osisRef="Isa.37.36">Isa 37:36</reference>). Libnah, according to the Onom. a place <hi type="italic">in regione Eleutheropolitana</hi>, is probably the same as <hi type="italic">Tell es-Safieh</hi> (“hill of the pure” = of the white), to the north-west of <hi type="italic">Bet Gibrin</hi>, called <hi type="italic">Alba Specula</hi> (<hi type="italic">Blanche Garde</hi>) in ten middle ages. The expression ויּשׁמע (“and he heard”), which occurs twice in the text, points back to what is past, and also prepares the way for what follows: “having heard this, he sent,” etc. At the same time it appears to have been altered from ויּשׁב.
entries.1af088a4a7f598a66d2c6f440900d31ebc3f96a1: <reference osisRef="Isa.37.10-Isa.37.13">Isa 37:10-13</reference> <div eID="gen13264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13265" type="x-p"/> The message. <hi type="italic">“Thus shall ye say to Hizkiyahu king of Judah, saying, Let not thy God in whom thou trustest deceive thee, saying, Jerusalem will not be given into the hand of the king of Asshur. Behold, thou hast surely heard what </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">that which</hi>)<hi type="italic">the kings of Asshur have done to all lands, to lay the ban upon them; and thou, thou shouldst be delivered?! Have the gods of the nations, which my fathers destroyed, delivered them: Gozan, and Haran, and Rezeph, and the Benē - ‛Eden , which are in Tellasar? Where is </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">where is he</hi>)<hi type="italic">the king of Hamath, and the king of Arpad, and the king of 'Ir-Sepharvaim, Hena', and 'Ivah?”</hi>Although ארץ is feminine, אותם (K. אתם), like להחרימם, points back to the lands (in accordance with the want of any thoroughly developed distinction of the genders in Hebrew); likewise אשׁר <hi type="italic">quas pessumdederunt</hi>. There is historical importance in the fact, that here Sennacherib attributes to his fathers (Sargon and the previous kings of the Derketade dynasty which he had overthrown) what Rabshakeh on the occasion of the first mission had imputed to Sennacherib himself. On Gozan, see p. 33. It is no doubt identical with the Zuzan of the Arabian geographers, which is described as a district of outer Armenia, situated on the <hi type="italic">Chabur</hi>, e.g., in the <hi type="italic">Merasid</hi>. (“The <hi type="italic">Chabur</hi> is the <hi type="italic">Chabur</hi> of <hi type="italic">el-Hasaniye</hi>, a district of <hi type="italic">Mosul</hi>, to the east of the Tigris; it comes down from the mountains of the land of Zuzan, flows through a broad and thickly populated country in the north of <hi type="italic">Mosul</hi>, which is called outer Armenia, and empties itself into the Tigris.” Ptolemy, on the other hand (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.18">Isa 37:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.14">Isa 37:14</reference>), is acquainted with a Mesopotamian <hi type="italic">Gauzanitis</hi>; and, looking upon northern Mesopotamia as the border land of Armenia, he says, κατέχει δὲ τῆς ξηώρας τὰ μὲν πρὸς τῆ Αρμενία ἡ Ανθεμουσία (not far from Edessa) ὑφ ἥν ἡ Χαλκῖτις ὑπὸ δὲ ταύτην ἡ Γαυζανῖτις, possibly the district of <hi type="italic">Gulzan</hi>, in which <hi type="italic">Nisibin</hi>, the ancient <hi type="italic">Nisibis</hi>, still stands.<note placement="foot">See Oppert, <hi type="italic">Expédition</hi>, i. 60.</note> <div eID="gen13265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13266" type="x-p"/> For <hi type="italic">Hârân</hi> (Syr. <hi type="italic">Horon</hi>; Joseph. <hi type="italic">Charran</hi> of Mesopotamia), the present <hi type="italic">Harrân</hi>, not far from <hi type="italic">Charmelik</hi>, see <hi type="italic">Genesis</hi>, p. 327. The <hi type="italic">Harran </hi>in the <hi type="italic">Guta</hi> of Damascus (on the southern arm of the <hi type="italic">Harus</hi>), which Beke has recently identified with it, is not connected with it in any way. <hi type="italic">Retseph</hi> is the <hi type="italic">Rhesapha</hi> of Ptol. v. 18, 6, below Thapsacus, the present <hi type="italic">Rusafa</hi> in the Euphrates-valley of <hi type="italic">ez-Zor</hi>, between the Euphrates and Tadmur (Palmyra; see Robinson, <hi type="italic">Pal</hi>.). <hi type="italic">Telassar</hi>, with which the Targum (ii. iii.) and Syr. confound the Ellasar of <reference osisRef="Gen.14.1">Gen 14:1</reference>, i.e., Artemita (Artamita), is not the <hi type="italic">Thelseae</hi> of the <hi type="italic">Itin. Antonini</hi> and of the <hi type="italic">Notitia dignitatum</hi> - in which case the <hi type="italic">Benē</hi>-<hi type="italic">‛Eden</hi> might be the tribe of <hi type="italic">Bêt Genn</hi> (Bettegene) on the southern slope of Lebanon (i.e., the 'Eden of Coelesyria, <reference osisRef="Amos.1.5">Amo 1:5</reference>; the <hi type="italic">Paradeisos</hi> of Ptol. v. 15, 20; <hi type="italic">Paradisus</hi>, Plin. v. 19) - but the <hi type="italic">Thelser</hi> of the <hi type="italic">Tab. Peuting.</hi>, on the eastern side of the Tigris; and <hi type="italic">Benē</hi>-<hi type="italic">‛Eden</hi> is the tribe of the <hi type="italic">'Eden</hi> mentioned by Ezekiel (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.23">Eze 27:23</reference>) after Haran and Ctesiphon. Consequently the enumeration of the warlike deeds describes a curve, which passes in a north-westerly direction through Hamath and Arpad, and then returns in Sepharvaim to the border of southern Mesopotamia and Babylonia. <hi type="italic">'Ir-Sepharvaim </hi>is like <hi type="italic">'Ir-Nâchâs</hi>, <hi type="italic">'Ir-shemesh</hi>, etc. The legends connect the name with the sacred books. The form of the name is inexplicable; but the name itself probably signifies the double shore (after the Aramaean), as the city, which was the southernmost of the leading places of Mesopotamia, was situated on the Euphrates. The words ועוּה הנע, if not take as proper names, would signify, “he has taken away, and overthrown;” but in that case we should expect ועוּוּ הניעוּ or ועוּיתי הניעתי. They are really the names of cities which it is no longer possible to trace. <hi type="italic">Hena'</hi> is hardly the well-known <hi type="italic">Avatho</hi> on the Euphrates, as Gesenius, V. Niebuhr, and others suppose; and <hi type="italic">'Ivah</hi>, the seat of the <hi type="italic">Avvı̄m</hi> (2Ki 17:31), agrees still less, so far as the sound of the word is concerned, with “the province of <hi type="italic">Hebeh</hi> (? <hi type="italic">Hebeb:</hi> Ritter, <hi type="italic">Erdk</hi>. xi. 707), situated between <hi type="italic">Anah</hi> and the <hi type="italic">Chabur</hi> on the Euphrates,” with which V. Niebuhr combines it.<note placement="foot">For other combinations of equal value, see Oppert, <hi type="italic">Expédition</hi>, i. 220.</note>
entries.70df73981520339a9d0368b8ac69f05d412ee22d: <reference osisRef="Isa.37.14-Isa.37.20">Isa 37:14-20</reference> <div eID="gen13266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13267" type="x-p"/> This intimidating message, which declared the God of Israel to be utterly powerless, was conveyed by the messengers of Sennacherib in the form of a latter. <hi type="italic">“And Hizkiyahu took the letter out of the hand of the messengers, and read it </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">read them</hi>)<hi type="italic">, and went up to the house of Jehovah; and Hizkiyahu spread it before Jehovah.”</hi> <hi type="italic">Sephârı̄m</hi> (the sheets) is equivalent to <hi type="italic">the letter</hi> (not a letter <hi type="italic">in duplo</hi>), like <hi type="italic">literae</hi> (cf., <hi type="italic">grammata</hi>). ויּקראהוּ (changed by K. into m- ') is construed according to the singular idea. Thenius regards this spreading out of the letter as a <hi type="italic">naiveté</hi>; and Gesenius even goes so far as to speak of the praying machines of the Buddhists. But it was simply prayer without words - an act of prayer, which afterwards passed into vocal prayer. <hi type="italic">“And Hizkiyahu prayed to </hi>(K. <hi type="italic">before</hi>)<hi type="italic">Jehovah, saying </hi>(K. <hi type="italic">and said</hi>),<hi type="italic">Jehovah of hosts </hi>(K. omits <hi type="italic">tsebhâ'ōth</hi>),<hi type="italic">God of Israel, enthroned upon the cherubim, Thou, yea Thou alone, art God of all the kingdoms of the earth; Thou, Thou hast made the heavens and the earth. Incline Thine ear, Jehovah, and hear </hi>וּשׁמע, various reading in both texts וּשׁמע)! <hi type="italic">Open Thine eyes </hi>(K. with <hi type="italic">Yod</hi> of the plural),<hi type="italic">Jehovah, and see; and hear the</hi> (K. <hi type="italic">all the</hi>)<hi type="italic">words of Sennacherib, which he hath sent </hi>(K. <hi type="italic">with which he hath sent him,</hi> i.e., Rabshakeh)<hi type="italic">to despise the living God! Truly, O Jehovah, the kings of Asshur have laid waste all lands, and their land </hi>(K. <hi type="italic">the nations and their land</hi>),<hi type="italic">and have put </hi>(<hi type="italic">venâthōn</hi>, K. <hi type="italic">venâthenū</hi>)<hi type="italic">their gods into the fire: for they were not gods, only the work of men’s hands, wood and stone; therefore they have destroyed them. And now, Jehovah our God, help us </hi>(K. adds <hi type="italic">pray</hi>)<hi type="italic">out of his hand, and all the kingdoms of the earth may know that Thou Jehovah </hi>(K. <hi type="italic">Jehovah Elohim</hi>)<hi type="italic">art it alone.”</hi> On כּרבים (no doubt the same word as γρυπές, though not fabulous beings like these, but a symbolical representation of heavenly beings), see my <hi type="italic">Genesis</hi>, p. 626; and on <hi type="italic">yōshēbh hakkerubhı̄m</hi> (enthroned on the cherubim), see at <reference osisRef="Ps.18.11">Psa 18:11</reference> and Psa 80:2. הוּא in אתּה־הוּא is an emphatic repetition, that is to say a strengthening, of the subject, like <reference osisRef="Isa.43.25">Isa 43:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.12">Isa 51:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.28">2Sa 7:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.12">Jer 49:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.44.5">Psa 44:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.9.6-Neh.9.7">Neh 9:6-7</reference>; Ezr 5:11 : <hi type="italic">tu ille</hi> (not <hi type="italic">tu es ille</hi>, Ges. §121, 2) = <hi type="italic">tu</hi>, <hi type="italic">nullus alius</hi>. Such passages as <reference osisRef="Isa.41.4">Isa 41:4</reference>, where הוּא is the predicate, do not belong here. עין is not a singular (like עיני in <reference osisRef="Ps.32.8">Psa 32:8</reference>, where the lxx have עיני), but a defective plural, as we should expect after <hi type="italic">pâqach</hi>. On the other hand, the reading <hi type="italic">shelâchō</hi> (“hath sent him”), which cannot refer to <hi type="italic">debhârı̄m</hi> (the words), but only to the person bringing the written message, is to be rejected. Moreover, Knobel cannot help giving up his preference for the reading <hi type="italic">venâthōn</hi> (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.41.43">Gen 41:43</reference>; Ges. §131, 4 <hi type="italic">a</hi>); just as, on the other hand, we cannot help regarding the reading ואת־ארצם את־כּל־הארצות as a mistake, when compared with the reading of the book of Kings. Abravanel explains the passage thus: “The Assyrians have devastated the lands, and <hi type="italic">their</hi> own land” (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.14.20">Isa 14:20</reference>), of which we may find examples in the list of victories given above; compare also <hi type="italic">Beth-arbel</hi> in Hos 10:14, if this is <hi type="italic">Irbil</hi> on the Tigris, from which Alexander’s second battle in Persia, which was really fought at Gaugamela, derived its name. But how does this tally with the fact that they threw the gods of these lands - that is to say, of their own land also (for אלהיהם could not possibly refer to הארצות, to the exclusion of ארצם) - into the fire? If we read <hi type="italic">haggōyı̄m</hi> (the nations), we get rid both of the reference to their own land, which is certainly purposeless here, and also of the otherwise inevitable conclusion that they burned the gods of their own country. The reading הארצות appears to have arisen from the fact, that after the verb החריב the lands appeared to follow more naturally as the object, than the tribes themselves (compare, however, <reference osisRef="Isa.60.12">Isa 60:12</reference>). The train of thought is the following: The Assyrians have certainly destroyed nations and their gods, because these gods were nothing but the works of men: do Thou then help us, O Jehovah, that the world may see that Thou alone art it, viz., God (<hi type="italic">'Elōhı̄m</hi>, as K. adds, although, according to the accents, Jehovah Elohim are connected together, as in the books of Samuel and Chronicles, and very frequently in the mouth of David: see <hi type="italic">Symbolae in Psalmos</hi>, pp. 15, 16).
entries.b2255935a2b33a7597a4dc8aca28456b71175bd4: <reference osisRef="Isa.37.21-Isa.37.23">Isa 37:21-23</reference> <div eID="gen13267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13268" type="x-p"/> The prophet’s reply. <hi type="italic">“And Isaiah the son of Amoz sent to Hizkiyahu, saying, Thus saith Jehovah the God of Israel, That which thou hast prayed to me concerning Sennacherib the king of Asshur </hi>(K. adds,<hi type="italic">I have heard</hi>)<hi type="italic">: this is the utterance which Jehovah utters concerning him.”</hi> He sent, i.e., sent a message, viz., by one of his disciples (<hi type="italic">limmūdı̄m</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.16">Isa 8:16</reference>). According to the text of Isaiah, אשׁר would commence the protasis to הדּבר זה (as for that which - this is the utterance); or, as the <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> of the apodosis is wanting, it might introduce relative clauses to what precedes (“I, to whom:” Ges. §123, 1, Anm. 1). But both of these are very doubtful. We cannot dispense with שׁמעתּי (I have heard), which is given by both the lxx and Syr. in the text of Isaiah, as well as that of Kings. <div eID="gen13268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13269" type="x-p"/> The prophecy of Isaiah which follows here, is in all respects one of the most magnificent that we meet with. It proceeds with strophe-like strides on the cothurnus of the Deborah style: <hi type="italic">“The virgin daughter of Zion despiseth thee, laugheth thee to scorn; the daughter of Jerusalem shaketh her head after thee. Whom hast thou reviled and blasphemed, and over whom hast thou spoken loftily, that thou hast lifted up thine eyes on high? Against the Holy One of Israel.”</hi> The predicate is written at the head, in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.37.22">Isa 37:22</reference></hi>, in the masculine, i.e., without any precise definition; since בּזה is a verb ל ה, and neither the participle nor the third pers. fem. of בּוּז. Zion is called a virgin, with reference to the shame with which it was threatened though without success (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.12">Isa 23:12</reference>); <hi type="italic">bethūlath</hi> <hi type="italic">bath</hi> are subordinate appositions, instead of co-ordinate. With a contented and heightened self-consciousness, she shakes her head behind him as he retreats with shame, saying by her attitude, as she moves her head backwards and forwards, that it must come to this, and could not be otherwise (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.16">Jer 18:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.15-Lam.2.16">Lam 2:15-16</reference>). The question in <reference osisRef="Isa.37.23">Isa 37:23</reference> reaches as far as עיניך, although, according to the accents, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.23">Isa 37:23</reference> is an affirmative clause: “and thou turnest thine eyes on high against the Holy One of Israel” (Hitzig, Ewald, Drechsler, and Keil). The question is put for the purpose of saying to Asshur, that He at whom they scoff is the God of Israel, whose pure holiness breaks out into a consuming fire against all by whom it is dishonoured. The <hi type="italic">fut. cons.</hi> ותּשּׂה is essentially the same as in <reference osisRef="Isa.51.12-Isa.51.13">Isa 51:12-13</reference>, and מרום is the same as in Isa 40:26.
entries.ee346f3f3490175d9414d80fe9a456628ef77853: <reference osisRef="Isa.37.24">Isa 37:24</reference> <div eID="gen13269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13270" type="x-p"/> Second turn, <hi type="italic">“By thy servants </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">thy messengers</hi>)<hi type="italic">hast thou reviled the Lord, in that thou sayest, With the multitude </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">chethib </hi>ברכב)<hi type="italic">of my chariots have I climbed the height of the mountains, the inner side of Lebanon; and I shall fell the lofty growth of its cedars, the choice </hi>(<hi type="italic">mibhchar , </hi> K.<hi type="italic">mibhchōr</hi>)<hi type="italic">of its cypresses: and I shall penetrate </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">and will penetrate</hi>)<hi type="italic">to the height </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">the halting-place</hi>)<hi type="italic">of its uttermost border, the grove of its orchard.”</hi> The other text appears, for the most part, the preferable one here. Whether <hi type="italic">mal'ăkhekhâ</hi> (thy messengers, according to <reference osisRef="Isa.9.14">Isa 9:14</reference>) or <hi type="italic">‛ăbhâdekhâ</hi> (thy servants, viz., Rabshakeh, Tartan, and Rabsaris) is to be preferred, may be left undecided; also whether רכבי ברכב is an error or a superlative expression, “with chariots of my chariots,” i.e., my countless chariots; also, thirdly, whether Isaiah wrote <hi type="italic">mibhchōr</hi>. He uses <hi type="italic">mistōr</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.4.6">Isa 4:6</reference> for a special reason; but such obscure forms befit in other instances the book of Kings, with its colouring of northern Palestine; and we also meet with <hi type="italic">mibhchōr</hi> in 2Ki 3:19, in the strongly Aramaic first series of histories of Elisha. On the other hand, קצּה מלון is certainly the original reading, in contrast with קצו מרום. It is important, as bearing upon the interpretation of the passage, that both texts have ואכרת, not ואכרת, and that the other text confirms this pointing, inasmuch as it has ואבואה instead of ואובא. The Lebanon here, if not purely emblematical (as in <reference osisRef="Jer.22.6">Jer 22:6</reference> = the royal city Jerusalem; <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.3">Eze 17:3</reference> = Judah-Jerusalem), has at any rate a synecdochical meaning (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.14.8">Isa 14:8</reference>), signifying the land of Lebanon, i.e., the land of Israel, into which he had forced a way, and all the fortresses and great men of which he would destroy. He would not rest till Jerusalem, the most renowned height of the land of Lebanon, was lying at his feet. Thenius is quite right in regarding the “resting-place of the utmost border” and “the pleasure-garden wood” as containing allusions to the holy city and its royal citadel (compare the allegory in chapter 5).
entries.c37e07449a203e9c1f9f0f4d23e0cb7bf5797147: <reference osisRef="Isa.37.25">Isa 37:25</reference> <div eID="gen13270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13271" type="x-p"/> Third turn, <hi type="italic">“I, I have digged and drunk </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">foreign</hi>)<hi type="italic">waters, and will make dry with the sole of my feet all the Nile-arms </hi>(יארי, K. יאורי)<hi type="italic">of Matsor.”</hi> If we take עליתי in <reference osisRef="Isa.37.24">Isa 37:24</reference> as a perfect of certainty, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.37.25">Isa 37:25</reference></hi> would refer to the overcoming of the difficulties connected with the barren sandy steppe on the way to Egypt (viz., <hi type="italic">et - Tih</hi>); but the perfects stand out against the following futures, as statements of what was actually past. Thus, in places where there were no waters at all, and it might have been supposed that his army would inevitably perish, there he had dug them (<hi type="italic">qūr</hi>, from which <hi type="italic">mâqōr</hi> is derived, <hi type="italic">fodere</hi>; not <hi type="italic">scaturire</hi>, as Luzzatto supposes), and had drunk up these waters, which had been called up, as if by magic, upon foreign soil; and in places where there were waters, as in Egypt (<hi type="italic">mâtsōr</hi> is used in Isaiah and Micah for <hi type="italic">mitsrayim</hi>, with a play upon the appellative meaning of the word: an enclosing fence, a fortifying girdle: see <reference osisRef="Ps.31.22">Psa 31:22</reference>), the Nile-arms and canals of which appeared to bar all farther progress, it was an easy thing for him to set at nought all these opposing hindrances. The Nile, with its many arms, was nothing but a puddle to him, which he trampled out with his feet.
entries.e95546aadb4ccbe29335cedcfa6562da73dd3318: <reference osisRef="Isa.37.26-Isa.37.27">Isa 37:26-27</reference> <div eID="gen13271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13272" type="x-p"/> And yet what he was able to do was not the result of his own power, but of the counsel of God, which he subserved. Fourth turn, <hi type="italic">“Hast thou not heart? I have done it long ago, from </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">lemin , since</hi>)<hi type="italic">the days of ancient time have I formed it, and now brought it to pass </hi>(הבאתיה, K. הביאתיה):<hi type="italic">that thou shouldst lay waste fortified cities into desolate stone heaps; and their inhabitants, powerless, were terrified, and were put to shame </hi>(ובשׁוּ, K. ויּבשׁוּ):<hi type="italic">became herb of the field and green of the turf, herb of the house-tops, and a corn-field </hi>(וּשׁדמה, K. <hi type="italic">and blighted corn</hi>)<hi type="italic">before the blades.”</hi> <hi type="italic">L'mērâcōq</hi> (from afar) is not to be connected with the preceding words, but according to the parallel with those which follow. The historical reality, in this instance the Assyrian judgment upon the nations, had had from all eternity an ideal reality in God (see at <reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Isa 22:11</reference>). The words are addressed to the Assyrian; and as his instrumentality formed the essential part of the divine purpose, וּתהי does not mean “there should,” but “thou shouldest,” e!mellej e)chremw=sai (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.44.14-Isa.44.15">Isa 44:14-15</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Hab.1.17">Hab 1:17</reference>). K. has להשׁות instead of להשׁאות (though not as <hi type="italic">chethib</hi>, in which case it would have to be pointed להשׁות), a singularly syncopated <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi> (for לשׁאות). The point of comparison in the four figures is the facility with which they can be crushed. The nations in the presence of the Assyrian became, as it were, weak, delicate grasses, with roots only rooted in the surface, or like a cornfield with the stalk not yet formed (<hi type="italic">shedēmâh</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.8">Isa 16:8</reference>), which could easily be rooted up, and did not need to be cut down with the sickle. This idea is expressed still more strikingly in Kings, “like corn blighted (<hi type="italic">shedēphâh</hi>, compare <hi type="italic">shiddâpōn</hi>, corn-blight) before the shooting up of the stalk;” the Assyrian being regarded as a parching east wind, which destroys the seed before the stalk is formed.
entries.496bd934cf800bb7fdbb3054b913c6b28c06ecce: <reference osisRef="Isa.37.28-Isa.37.29">Isa 37:28-29</reference> <div eID="gen13272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13273" type="x-p"/> Asshur is Jehovah’s chosen instrument while thus casting down the nations, which are “short-handed against him,” i.e., incapable of resisting him. But Jehovah afterwards places this lion under firm restraint; and before it has reached the goal set before it, He leads it back into its own land, as if with a ring through its nostril. Fifth turn, <hi type="italic">“And thy sitting down, and thy going out, and thy entering in, I know; and thy heating thyself against me. On account of thy heating thyself against me, and because thy self-confidence has risen up into mine ears, I put my ring into thy nose, and my muzzle into thy lips, and lead thee back by the way by which thou hast come.”</hi> Sitting down and rising up (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.2">Psa 139:2</reference>), going out and coming in (<reference osisRef="Ps.121.8">Psa 121:8</reference>), denote every kind of human activity. All the thoughts and actions, the purposes and undertakings of Sennacherib, more especially with regard to the people of Jehovah, were under divine control. יען is followed by the infinitive, which is then continued in the finite verb, just as in Isa 30:12. שׁאננך (another reading, שׁאננך) is used as a substantive, and denotes the Assyrians’ complacent and scornful self-confidence (<reference osisRef="Ps.123.4">Psa 123:4</reference>), and has nothing to do with שׁאון (Targum, Abulw., Rashi, Kimchi, Rosenmüller, Luzzatto). The figure of the leading away with a nose-ring (<hi type="italic">chachı̄</hi> with a latent <hi type="italic">dagesh</hi>, חא to prick, hence <hi type="italic">chōach</hi>, Arab. <hi type="italic">chōch</hi>, <hi type="italic">chōcha</hi>, a narrow slit, literally means a cut or aperture) is repeated in Eze 38:4. Like a wild beast that had been subdued by force, the Assyrian would have to return home, without having achieved his purpose with Judah (or with Egypt).
entries.f79e9d643c8f15a4d44959f4e43957ced190357a: <reference osisRef="Isa.37.30">Isa 37:30</reference> <div eID="gen13273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13274" type="x-p"/> The prophet now turns to Hezekiah. <hi type="italic">“And let this be a sign to thee, Men eat this year what is self-sown; and in the second year what springs from the roots</hi> (shâc, K. sâchı̄sh);<hi type="italic">and in the third year they sow and reap and plant vineyards, and eat </hi>(<hi type="italic">chethib</hi> אכול)<hi type="italic">their fruit.”</hi> According to Thenius, <hi type="italic">hasshânâh</hi> (this year) signifies the first year after Sennacherib’s invasions, <hi type="italic">hasshânâh</hi> <hi type="italic">hasshēnı̄th</hi> (the second year) the current year in which the words were uttered by Hezekiah, <hi type="italic">hasshânâh</hi> <hi type="italic">hasshelı̄shith</hi> (the third year) the year that was coming in which the land would be cleared of the enemy. But understood in this way, the whole would have been no sign, but simply a prophecy that the condition of things during the two years was to come to an end in the third. It would only be a “sign” if the second year was also still in the future. By <hi type="italic">hasshânâh</hi>, therefore, we are to understand what the expression itself requires (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.29.1">Isa 29:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.10">Isa 32:10</reference>), namely the current year, in which the people had been hindered from cultivating their fields by the Assyrian who was then in the land, and therefore had been thrown back upon the <hi type="italic">sâphı̄ach</hi>, i.e., the after growth (αὐτόματα, lxx, the self-sown), or crop which had sprung up from the fallen grains of the previous harvest (from <hi type="italic">sâphach</hi>, <hi type="italic">adjicere</hi>, see at <reference osisRef="Hab.2.15">Hab 2:15</reference>; or, according to others, <hi type="italic">effundere</hi>). It was autumn at the time when Isaiah gave this sign (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.9">Isa 33:9</reference>), and the current civil year was reckoned from one autumnal equinox to the other, as, for example, in <reference osisRef="Exod.23.16">Exo 23:16</reference>, where the feast of tabernacles or harvest festival is said to fall at the close of the year; so that if the fourteenth year of Hezekiah was the year 714, the current year would extend from Tishri 714 to Tishri 713. But if in the next year also, 713-712, there was no sowing and reaping, but the people were to eat <hi type="italic">shâchis</hi>, i.e., that which grew of itself (αὐτοφυές, Aq., Theod.), and that very sparingly, not from the grains shed at the previous harvest, but from the roots of the wheat, we need not assume that this year, 713-712, happened to be a sabbatical year, in which the law required all agricultural pursuits to be suspended.<note placement="foot">There certainly is no necessity for a sabbatical year followed by a year of jubilee, to enable us to explain the “sign,” as Hofmann supposes.</note> <div eID="gen13274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13275" type="x-p"/> It is very improbable in itself that the prophet should have included a circumstance connected with the calendar in his “sign;” and, moreover, according to the existing chronological data, the year 715 had been a sabbatical year (see Hitzig). It is rather presupposed, either that the land would be too thoroughly devastated and desolate for the fields to be cultivated and sown (Keil); or, as we can hardly imagine such an impossibility as this, if we picture to ourselves the existing situation and the kind of agriculture common in Palestine, that the Assyrian would carry out his expedition to Egypt in this particular year (713-12), and returning through Judah, would again prevent the sowing of the corn (Hitzig, Knobel). But in the third year, that is to say the year 712-11, freedom and peace would prevail again, and there would be nothing more to hinder the cultivation of the fields or vineyards. If this should be the course of events during the three years, it would be a sign to king Hezekiah that the fate of the Assyrian would be no other than that predicated. The year 712-11 would be the peremptory limit appointed him, and the year of deliverance.
entries.d2c06c230557f994af564105cfd2fed69088f0b9: <reference osisRef="Isa.37.31-Isa.37.32">Isa 37:31-32</reference> <div eID="gen13275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13276" type="x-p"/> Seventh turn, <hi type="italic">“And that which is escaped of the house of Judah, that which remains will again take root downward, and bear fruit upward. For from Jerusalem will a remnant go forth, and a fugitive from Mount Zion; the zeal of Jehovah of hosts </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">chethib </hi>omits<hi type="italic">tsebhâ'ōth</hi>)<hi type="italic">will carry this out.”</hi> The agricultural prospect of the third year shapes itself there into a figurative representation of the fate of Judah. Isaiah’s watchword, “a remnant shall return,” is now fulfilled; Jerusalem has been spared, and becomes the source of national rejuvenation. You year the echo of <reference osisRef="Isa.5.24">Isa 5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Isa 9:6</reference>, and also of Isa 27:6. The word <hi type="italic">tsebhâ'ōth</hi> is wanting in Kings, here as well as in <reference osisRef="Isa.37.17">Isa 37:17</reference>; in fact, this divine name is, as a rule, very rare in the book of Kings, where it only occurs in the first series of accounts of Elijah (1Ki 18:15; 1Ki 19:10, 1Ki 19:14; cf., 2Ki 3:14).
entries.4583fe6572c5ef1e2e350510ca531059235ebc8c: <reference osisRef="Isa.37.33-Isa.37.35">Isa 37:33-35</reference> <div eID="gen13276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13277" type="x-p"/> The prophecy concerning the protection of Jerusalem becomes more definite in the last turn than it ever has been before. <hi type="italic">“Therefore thus saith Jehovah concerning the king of Asshur, He will not enter into this city, nor shoot off an arrow there; nor do they assault it with a shield, nor cast up earthworks against it. By the way by which he came </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">will come</hi>)<hi type="italic">will he return; and he will not enter into this city, saith Jehovah. And I shield this city </hi>(על, K. אל)<hi type="italic">, to help it, for mine own sake, and for the sake of David my servant.”</hi> According to Hitzig, this conclusion belongs to the later reporter, on account of its “suspiciously definite character.” Knobel, on the other hand, sees no reason for disputing the authorship of Isaiah, inasmuch as in all probability the pestilence had already set in (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.24">Isa 33:24</reference>), and threatened to cripple the Assyrian army very considerably, so that the prophet began to hope that Sennacherib might now be unable to stand against the powerful Ethiopian king. To us, however, the words “Thus saith Jehovah” are something more than a flower of speech; and we hear the language of a man exalted above the standard of the natural man, and one how has been taken, as Amos says (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.7">Amo 3:7</reference>), by God, the moulder of history into “His secret.” Here also we see the prophecy at its height, towards which it has been ascending from <reference osisRef="Isa.6.13">Isa 6:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.10.33-Isa.10.34">Isa 10:33-34</reference> onwards, through the midst of obstacles accumulated by the moral condition of the nation, but with the same goal invariably in view. The Assyrian will not storm Jerusalem; there will not even be preparations for a siege. The verb <hi type="italic">qiddēm</hi> is construed with a double accusative, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.21.4">Psa 21:4</reference> : <hi type="italic">sōlelâh</hi> refers to the earthworks thrown up for besieging purposes, as in Jer 32:24. The reading יבא instead of בּא has arisen in consequence of the eye having wandered to the following יבא. The promise in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.37.35">Isa 37:35</reference></hi> sounds like Isa 31:5. The reading אל for על is incorrect. One motive assigned (“for my servant David’s sake”) is the same as in 1Ki 15:4, etc.; and the other (“for mine own sake”) the same as in <reference osisRef="Isa.43.25">Isa 43:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.11">Isa 48:11</reference> (compare, however, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Isa 55:3</reference> also). On the one hand, it is in accordance with the honour and faithfulness of Jehovah, that Jerusalem is delivered; and, on the other hand, it is the worth of David, or, what is the same thing, the love of Jehovah turned towards him, of which Jerusalem reaps the advantage.
entries.5a04d5bbde6138c934ba4aa192c7a2e35c035110: <reference osisRef="Isa.37.36-Isa.37.38">Isa 37:36-38</reference> <div eID="gen13277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13278" type="x-p"/> To this culminating prophecy there is now appended an account of the catastrophe itself. <hi type="italic">“Then </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">And it came to pass that night, that</hi>)<hi type="italic">the angel of Jehovah went forth and smote </hi>(<hi type="italic">vayyakkeh , </hi> K.<hi type="italic">vayyakh</hi>)<hi type="italic">in the camp of Asshur a hundred and eighty-five thousand; and when men rose up in the morning, behold, they were all lifeless corpses. Then Sennacherib king of Asshur decamped, and went forth and returned, and settled down in Nineveh. And it cam to pass, as he was worshipping in the temple of Misroch, his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons </hi>(L.<hi type="italic">chethib</hi> omits <hi type="italic">'his sons'</hi>)<hi type="italic">smote him with the sword; and when they escaped to the land of Ararat, Esarhaddon ascended the throne in his stead.”</hi> The first pair of histories closes here with a short account of the result of the Assyrian drama, in which Isaiah’s prophecies were most gloriously fulfilled: not only the prophecies immediately preceding, but all the prophecies of the Assyrian era since the time of Ahaz, which pointed to the destruction of the Assyrian forces (e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.10.33-Isa.10.34">Isa 10:33-34</reference>), and to the flight and death of the king of Assyrian (<reference osisRef="Isa.31.9">Isa 31:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Isa 30:33</reference>). If we look still further forward to the second pair of histories (chapters 38-39), we see from <reference osisRef="Isa.38.6">Isa 38:6</reference> that it is only by anticipation that the account of these closing events is finished here; for the third history carries us back to the period before the final catastrophe. We may account in some measure for the haste and brevity of this closing historical fragment, from the prophet’s evident wish to finish up the history of the Assyrian complications, and the prophecy bearing upon it. But if we look back, there is a gap between <reference osisRef="Isa.37.36">Isa 37:36</reference> and the event narrated here. For, according to <reference osisRef="Isa.37.30">Isa 37:30</reference>, there was to be an entire year of trouble between the prophecy and the fulfilment, during which the cultivation of the land would be suspended. What took place during that year? There can be no doubt that Sennacherib was engaged with Egypt; for (1.) when he made his second attempt to get Jerusalem into his power, he had received intelligence of the advance of Tirhakah, and therefore had withdrawn the centre of his army from Lachish, and encamped before Libnah (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.8-Isa.37.9">Isa 37:8-9</reference>); (2.) according to Josephus (<hi type="italic">Ant.</hi> x. 1, 4), there was a passage of Berosus, which has been lost, in which he stated that Sennacherib “made an expedition against all Asia and Egypt;” (3.) Herodotus relates (ii. 141) that, after Anysis the blind, who lost his throne for fifty years in consequence of an invasion of Egypt by the Ethiopians under Sabakoa, but who recovered it again, Sethon the priest of Hephaestus ascended the throne. The priestly caste was so oppressed by him, that when Sanacharibos, the king of the Arabians and Assyrians, led a great army against Egypt, they refused to perform their priestly functions. but the priest-king went into the temple to pray, and his God promised to help him. He experienced the fulfilment of this prophecy before Pelusium, where the invasion was to take place, and where he awaited the foe with such as continued true to him. “Immediately after the arrival of Sanacharibos, an army of field-mice swarmed throughout the camp of the foe, and devoured their quivers, bows, and shield-straps, so that when morning came on they had to flee without arms, and lost many men in consequence. This is the origin of the stone of Sethon in the temple of Hephaestus (at Memphis), which is standing there still, with a mouse in one hand, and with this inscription: Whosoever looks at me, let him fear the gods!” This Σέθως (possibly the <hi type="italic">Zet</hi> whose name occurs in the lists at the close of the twenty-third dynasty, and therefore in the wrong place) is to be regarded as one of the Saitic princes of the twenty-sixth dynasty, who seem to have ruled in Lower Egypt contemporaneously with the Ethiopians<note placement="foot">A seal of Pharaoh <hi type="italic">Sabakon</hi> has been found among the ruins of the palace of Kuyunjik. The colossal image of <hi type="italic">Tarakos</hi> is found among the bas-reliefs of Mediet-Habu. He is holding firmly a number of Asiatic prisoners by the hair of their head, and threatening them with a club. There are several other stately monuments in imitation of the Egyptian style in the ruins of Nepata, the northern capital of the Meriotic state, which belong to him (Lepsius, <hi type="italic">Denkmäler</hi>, p. 10 of the programme).</note> (as, in fact, is stated in a passage of the Armenian Eusebius, <hi type="italic">Aethiopas et Saitas regnasse aiunt eodem tempore</hi>), until they succeeded at length in ridding themselves of the hateful supremacy. Herodotus evidently depended in this instance upon the hearsay of Lower Egypt, which transferred the central point of the Assyrian history to their own native princely house. The question, whether the disarming of the Assyrian army in front of Pelusium merely rested upon a legendary interpretation of the mouse in Sethon’s hand,<note placement="foot">This Sethos monument has not yet been discovered (Brugsch, <hi type="italic">Reiseberichte</hi>, p. 79). The temple of Phta was on the south side of Memphis; the site is marked by the ruins at Mitrahenni.</note> which may possibly have been originally intended as a symbol of destruction; or whether it was really founded upon an actual occurrence which was exaggerated in the legend,<note placement="foot">The inhabitants of Troas worshipped <hi type="italic">mice</hi>, “because they gnawed the strings of the enemies’ bows” (see Wesseling on <hi type="italic">Il</hi>. i. 39).</note> may be left undecided. <div eID="gen13278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13279" type="x-p"/> But it is a real insult to Isaiah, when Thenius and G. Rawlinson place the scene of <reference osisRef="Isa.37.36">Isa 37:36</reference> at Pelusium, and thus give the preference to Herodotus. Has not Isaiah up to this point constantly prophesied that the power of Asshur was to be broken in the holy mountain land of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.25">Isa 14:25</reference>), that the Lebanon forest of the Assyrian army would break to pieces before Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.32-Isa.10.34">Isa 10:32-34</reference>), and that there the Assyrian camp would become the booty of the inhabitants of the city, and that without a conflict? And is not the catastrophe that would befal Assyria described in <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1-Isa.18.7">Isa 18:1-7</reference> as an act of Jehovah, which would determine the Ethiopians to do homage to God who was enthroned upon Zion? We need neither cite <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.21">2Ch 32:21</reference> nor <reference osisRef="Ps.76.1-Ps.76.12">Psa 76:1-12</reference> (lxx ὠδὴ πρὸς τὸν Ἀσσύριον), according to which the weapons of Asshur break to pieces upon Jerusalem; Isaiah’s prophecies are quite sufficient to prove, that to force this Pelusiac disaster<note placement="foot">G. Rawlinson, <hi type="italic">Monarchies</hi>, ii. 445.</note> into <reference osisRef="Isa.37.36">Isa 37:36</reference> is a most thoughtless concession to Herodotus. The final catastrophe occurred before Jerusalem, and the account in Herodotus gives us no certain information even as to the issue of the Egyptian campaign, which took place in the intervening year. Such a gap as the one which occurs before <reference osisRef="Isa.37.36">Isa 37:36</reference> is not without analogy in the historical writings of the Bible; see, for example, Num 20:1, where an abrupt leap is made over the thirty-seven years of the wanderings in the desert. The abruptness is not affected by the addition of the clause in the book of Kings, “It came to pass that night.” For, in the face of the “sign” mentioned in <reference osisRef="Isa.37.30">Isa 37:30</reference>, this cannot mean “in that very night” (viz., the night following the answer given by Isaiah); but (unless it is a careless interpolation) it must refer to <reference osisRef="Isa.37.33">Isa 37:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.34">Isa 37:34</reference>, and mean <hi type="italic">illa nocte</hi>, viz., the night in which the Assyrian had encamped before Jerusalem. The account before us reads just like that of the slaying of the first-born in Egypt (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.12">Exo 12:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.11.4">Exo 11:4</reference>). The plague of Egypt is marked as a pestilence by the use of the word <hi type="italic">nâgaph</hi> in connection with <hi type="italic">hikkâh</hi> in <reference osisRef="Exod.12.23">Exo 12:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.13">Exo 12:13</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.4.10">Amo 4:10</reference>, where it seems to be alluded to under the name דּבר); and in the case before us also we cannot think of anything else than a divine judgment of this kind, which even to the present day defies all attempts at an aetiological solution, and which is described in 2 Sam as effected through the medium of angels, just as it is here. Moreover, the concise brevity of the narrative leaves it quite open to assume, as Hensler and others do, that the ravages of the pestilence in the Assyrian army, which carried off thousands in the night (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.6">Psa 91:6</reference>), even to the number of 185,000, may have continued for a considerable time.<note placement="foot">The pestilence in Mailand in 1629 carried off, according to Tadino, 160,000 men; that in Vienna, in 1679, 122,849; that in Moscow, at the end of the last century, according to Martens, 670,000; but this was during the whole time that the ravages of the pestilence lasted.</note> <div eID="gen13279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13280" type="x-p"/> The main thing is the fact that the prophecy in <reference osisRef="Isa.31.8">Isa 31:8</reference> was actually fulfilled. According to Josephus (<hi type="italic">Ant.</hi> x. 1, 5), when Sennacherib returned from his unsuccessful Egyptian expedition, he found the detachment of his army, which he had left behind in Palestine, in front of Jerusalem, where a pestilential disease sent by God was making great havoc among the soldiers, and that on the very first night of the siege. The three verses, “he broke up, and went away, and returned home,” depict the hurried character of the retreat, like “<hi type="italic">abiit excessit evasit erupit</hi>” (Cic. ii. <hi type="italic">Catil. init.</hi>). The form of the sentence in <reference osisRef="Isa.37.38">Isa 37:38</reference> places Sennacherib’s act of worship and the murderous act of his sons side by side, as though they had occurred simultaneously. The connection would be somewhat different if the reading had been ויּכּהוּ (cf., Ewald, §341,<hi type="italic">a</hi>).<hi type="italic">Nisroch</hi> apparently signifies the eagle-like, or hawk-like (from <hi type="italic">nisr</hi>, <hi type="italic">nesher</hi>), possibly like “Arioch from <hi type="italic">'ărı̄</hi>. (The lxx transcribe it νασαραχ, A. ασαραχ, א ασαρακ (K. ἐσθραχ, where B. has μεσεραχ), and explorers of the monuments imagined at one time that they had discovered this god as <hi type="italic">Asarak</hi>;<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society</hi>, xii. 2, pp. 426-7.</note> but they have more recently retracted this, although there really is a hawk-headed figure among the images of the Assyrian deities or genii.<note placement="foot">Rawlinson, <hi type="italic">Monarchies</hi>, ii. 265.</note> <div eID="gen13280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13281" type="x-p"/> The name has nothing to do with that of the supreme Assyrian deity, <hi type="italic">Asur</hi>, <hi type="italic">Asshur</hi>. A better derivation of <hi type="italic">Nisroch</hi> would be from סרך, שׂרך, שׂרג; and this is confirmed by Oppert, who has discovered among the inscriptions in the harem of Khorsabad a prayer of Sargon to Nisroch, who appears there, like the Hymen of Greece, as the patron of marriage, and therefore as a “uniter.”<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Expédition Scientifique en Mesopotamie</hi>, t. ii. p. 339.</note> <div eID="gen13281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13282" type="x-p"/> The name <hi type="italic">'Adrammelekh</hi> (a god in 2Ki 17:31) signifies, as we now known, <hi type="italic">gloriosus</hi> (<hi type="italic">'addı̄r</hi>) <hi type="italic">est rex</hi>;” and <hi type="italic">Sharetser</hi> (for which we should expect to find <hi type="italic">Saretser</hi>), <hi type="italic">dominator tuebitur</hi>. The Armenian form of the latter name (in Moses Chroen. i. 23), <hi type="italic">San-asar</hi> (by the side of <hi type="italic">Adramel</hi>, who is also called <hi type="italic">Arcamozan</hi>), probably yields the original sense of “<hi type="italic">Lunus</hi> (the moon-god <hi type="italic">Sin</hi>) <hi type="italic">tuebitur</hi>.” Polyhistorus (in Euseb. <hi type="italic">chron. arm.</hi> p. 19), on the authority of Berosus, mentions only the former, <hi type="italic">Ardumuzan</hi>, as the murderer, and gives eighteen years as the length of Sennacherib’s reign. The murder did not take place immediately after his return, as Josephus says (<hi type="italic">Ant.</hi> x. 1, 5; cf., Tobit i. 21-25, Vulg.); and the expression used by Isaiah, he “dwelt (settled down) in Nineveh,” suggests the idea of a considerable interval. This interval embraced the suppression of the rebellion in Babylon, where Sennacherib made his son <hi type="italic">Asordan</hi> king, and the campaign in Cilicia (both from Polyhistorus),<note placement="foot">Vid., Richter, <hi type="italic">Berosi quae supersunt</hi> (1825), p. 62; Müller, <hi type="italic">Fragmenta Hist. Gr</hi>. ii. 504.</note> and also, according to the monuments, wars both by sea and land with Susiana, which supported the Babylonian thirst for independence. The <hi type="italic">Asordan</hi> of Polyhistorus is <hi type="italic">Esar-haddon</hi> (also written without the <hi type="italic">makkeph</hi>, <hi type="italic">Esarhaddon</hi>), which is generally supposed to be the Assyrian form of אשׁור־ח־ידן, <hi type="italic">Assur fratrem dedit</hi>. It is so difficult to make the chronology tally here, that Oppert, on <reference osisRef="Isa.36.1">Isa 36:1</reference>, proposes to alter the fourteenth year into the twenty-ninth, and Rawlinson would alter it into the twenty-seventh.<note placement="foot">Sargonides, p. 10, and <hi type="italic">Monarchies</hi>, ii. 434.</note> <div eID="gen13282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13283" type="x-p"/> They both of them assign to king Sargon a reign of seventeen (eighteen) years, and to Sennacherib (in opposition to Polyhistorus) a reign of twenty-three (twenty-four) years; and they both agree in giving 680 as the year of Sennacherib’s death. This brings us down below the first decade of Manasseh’s reign, and would require a different author from Isaiah for <reference osisRef="Isa.37.37">Isa 37:37</reference>, Isa 37:38. But the accounts given by Polyhistorus, Abydenus, and the astronomical canon, however we may reconcile them among themselves, do not extend the reign of Sennacherib beyond 693.<note placement="foot">See Duncker, Gesch. des Alterthums. i. pp. 708-9.</note> <div eID="gen13283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13284" type="x-p"/> It is true that even then Isaiah would have been at least about ninety years old. But the tradition which represents him as dying a martyr’s death in the reign of Manasseh, does really assign him a most unusual old age. Nevertheless, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.37">Isa 37:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.38">Isa 37:38</reference> may possibly have been added by a later hand. The two parricides fled to the “land of Ararat,” i.e., to Central Armenia. The Armenian history describes them as the founders of the tribes of the Sassunians and Arzerunians. From the princely house of the latter, among whom the name of Sennacherib was a very common one, sprang Leo the Armenian, whom Genesios describes as of Assyrio-Armenian blood. If this were the case, there would be no less than ten Byzantine emperors who were descendants of Sennacherib, and consequently it would not be till a very late period that the prophecy of Nahum was fulfilled.<note placement="foot">Duncker, on the contrary (p. 709), speaks of the parricides as falling very shortly afterwards by their brother’s hand, and overlooks the Armenian tradition (cf., Rawlinson, <hi type="italic">Monarchies</hi>, ii. 465), which transfers the flight of the two, who were to have been sacrificed, as is reported by their own father, to the year of the world 4494, i.e., b.c. 705 (see the historical survey of Prince Hubbof in the <hi type="italic">Miscellaneous Translations</hi>, vol. ii. 1834). The Armenian historian Thomas (at the end of the ninth century) expressly states that he himself had sprung from the Arzerunians, and therefore from Sennacherib; and for this reason his historical work is chiefly devoted to Assyrian affairs (see Aucher on Euseb. <hi type="italic">chron</hi>. i. p. xv.).</note>  <chapter eID="Isa.37"/> <div eID="gen13284" type="x-p"/>

entries.73af37817d78d7a1b165d234dc3d47f646fc988d: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.37.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.37.1" sID="gen47353" type="section"/> <div sID="gen47354" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi><hi type="italic"> And it came to pass. </hi>The Prophet declares that the only hope of safety that was left to the pious king was to bring his complaints before God as a righteous judge; as it is said in the Psalm, that<div eID="gen47354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47355" type="x-p"/>“in the same manner as servants or handmaids, when they are injured, look to the protection of their master or mistress, so the eyes of believers are fixed on the assistance of God.” — <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.123.2">Psalm 123:2</reference>.)<div eID="gen47355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47356" type="x-p"/>Thus, when Jerusalem appears to be completely ruined, Hezekiah, being bereft of earthly assistance, betakes himself to the protection of God, and thus acknowledges that there is no other remedy for heavy distresses. Hence also the grace of God shone more brightly, so that it was evidently miraculous, when the pious king was rescued from the jaws of that lion. We ought, therefore, to observe this circumstance, that we may better understand the great excellence of the work of God. Here we are also taught what we ought to do in the most desperate circumstances, not to be indolent or sluggish in supplicating the assistance of God, who himself invites us to come to him. We must not tremble or despair, but, on the contrary, ought to be stimulated by the necessity which presses upon us to seek his aid; as we see what Hezekiah did, who immediately betook himself to the temple in the same manner as to a place of safety, that he and all his people might take refuge under the shadow of God.<div eID="gen47356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47357" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">That King Hezekiah rent his clothes. </hi>He likewise adds the outward expressions of repentance, the “rending of the clothes and wearing sackcloth,” sprinkling of ashes, and other things of the same kind; for these were the ordinary signs of repentance, when, under the weight of any calamity by which they were afflicted, they confessed their guilt before God and implored pardon from him. Wonderful is the modesty of the holy king, who, after having performed so many illustrious works, and after having been adorned by the excellence of so many virtues, does not hesitate to prostrate himself humbly before God; and, on the other hand, wonderful is his courage and the steadfastness of his faith, in not being hindered by the weight of so heavy a temptation from freely seeking God by whom he was so severely smitten. Scarcely do we find one man in a hundred who does not murmur if God treats him with any degree of severity, who does not bring forward his good deeds as a ground of complaint, and remonstrate that he has been unjustly rewarded. Other men, when God does not comply with their wishes, complain that their worship of God has served no good purpose.<div eID="gen47357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47358" type="x-p"/>We perceive nothing of this kind in Hezekiah, who, though he is conscious of possessing uncommon piety, does not shrink from a confession of guilt, and therefore if we desire to turn away God’s anger, and to experience his favor in adversity, we must testify our repentance and sincerely acknowledge our guilt; for adversity does not fall out to us by chance, but is the method by which God arouses us to repentance. True, indeed, sackcloth and ashes will be of little avail, if they be not preceded by the inward feelings of the heart; for we know that hypocrites are abundantly liberal in the use of ceremonies; but as we have formerly said, the Holy Spirit justly commends those exercises, when they are directed to their proper object. And indeed it was a proof of uncommon piety and modesty, that the pious king and the whole nation excited themselves in this manner to fear God, and that he made a voluntary acknowledgment of guilt in a form attended by wretched filthiness; for we know how unwilling kings are to let themselves down from their rank.<div eID="gen47358" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.37.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen47353" osisID="Isa.37.1" type="section"/>
entries.7408ac16d1d8f1a59347897c5e8107bf761509c5: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.37.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.37.2" sID="gen47359" type="section"/> <div sID="gen47360" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi><hi type="italic"> And he sent Eliakim. </hi>This message was not intended merely to invite Isaiah to join with him in lamentation, but to request some consolation from his doctrine. And indeed to no purpose shall prayers be poured into the air, if they do not rest on the word of God. Thus we see that unbelievers are exceedingly noisy in their prayers, and yet they flee from God by despising or disregarding his promises. It was therefore a proof of sincere piety in Hezekiah, that, while he was earnestly employed in prayer, he at the same time added a confirmation of his hope, that he might not yield to temptation.<div eID="gen47360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47361" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">To Isaiah, the son of Amos the Prophet. </hi>He follows the method appointed by God, when he wishes to hear God speaking by the mouth of “the Prophet.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.18.15">Deuteronomy 18:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Mal.2.7">Malachi 2:7</reference>.) Though he relies on God alone, he does not reject the testimony of a mortal man; and therefore not without reason does he expressly add the designation <hi type="italic">Prophet; </hi>for he sends to Isaiah, that he may be confirmed by some new prediction, and names him, not as a private individual, but as the servant of God, whose duty it was to soothe the pious king by some consolation.<div eID="gen47361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47362" type="x-p"/>There are therefore two remedies that deserve our attention, by which we are soothed in affliction. First, we ought to call on God to deliver us; and, secondly, we ought to consult the prophets, at least, if we can obtain them, that they may bring us some comfort out of the word of God; for it is their duty to encourage and comfort the afflicted by promises, and if they fail to do so, still abundant consolation is communicated to us from the word. And we ought to consult the prophets, who were appointed, not only for their own age, but also for posterity and for every age; for although the men are dead, yet their books survive; their doctrine lives and shall never die. We shall never, therefore, be destitute of true remedies, if we do not reject them; but, in a word, we ought always to consult God.<div eID="gen47362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47363" type="x-p"/>It may be asked, “Was not Hezekiah abundantly supplied and fortified by the promises of God? Was it not a sign of distrust to seek new promises from the Prophet?” I reply, it ought not to be ascribed to unbelief or distrust, that he seeks a new promise; for, being conscious of his weakness, he does not scruple to ask new confirmations. The flesh always excites us to distrust, and therefore we ought not to despise additional aid; on the contrary, we ought always to seek every kind of assistance, by which we may resist various temptations; for on all sides Satan attacks and besieges us in such a manner that, if we are not strongly fortified, we shall scarcely be able to escape his snares and devices till the end. Although, therefore, we have been taught by the word of God that he will assist us in adversity, yet when we are engaged in any arduous contest, it is proper that we should again and again ask at the mouth of the Lord, and seek new confirmations for the purpose of strengthening our faith. There are indeed no prophecies of the same kind that are given to us in the present day; but we ought to apply to our use the general prophecies, which were also written for our benefit. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.15.4">Romans 15:4</reference>.)<div eID="gen47363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47364" type="x-p"/>As to the reason why Hezekiah sent ambassadors, and did not himself go to Isaiah, it was obviously because he was praying in the Temple; for the circumstance, that all the elders and counsellors were clothed with sackcloth, shews clearly that the mourning was general; and it is probable that prayers were publicly offered by the command of the king. Yet it ought to be observed, that the Prophet did not remain at home for his own ease or pleasure, but by his absence God intended to try the faith of the pious king.<div eID="gen47364" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.37.2" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen47359" osisID="Isa.37.2" type="section"/>
entries.ad636a947a00089ccb6a7865024bfdd2d10eb98b: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.37.4" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.37.4" sID="gen47365" type="section"/> <div sID="gen47366" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4.</hi><hi type="italic"> If perhaps Jehovah thy God will hear. </hi>Hezekiah appears to doubt whether, or not the Lord is willing to hear him; for the particle <foreign xml:lang="he">אולי</foreign> <hi type="italic">(ulai) </hi>is translated <hi type="italic">perhaps, </hi>and this is the meaning which it frequently bears in Scripture. But it ought to be observed that believers, even though they know with certainty that the Lord will assist them, yet, in consequence of being perplexed by the difficulty of the case, often speak in this manner. Hezekiah had reasons for hesitating, if we look at the matter itself; but when he turns his eyes to the word, he is made certain as to the will of God, so that he ceases to tremble. But as it is impossible that the flesh should not retard believers by making them walk in a halting and staggering manner, <note n="46"> <div sID="gen47367" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Tellement qu’ils ne marchent qu’en trainant les jambes ou a clochepied</foreign>,” “So that they walk only by dragging their limbs or limping.”<div eID="gen47367" type="x-p"/> </note> they sometimes accommodate their language to the present appearances of things.<div eID="gen47366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47368" type="x-p"/>It may also be observed, in other passages of Scripture, that the saints, even while speaking of what was certain, spoke in this manner; for Peter, in exhorting Simon, says,<div eID="gen47368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47369" type="x-p"/>“<hi type="italic">If</hi> <hi type="italic">perhaps </hi>this thought of thy heart may be forgiven thee.” <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.8.22">Acts 8:22</reference>.)<div eID="gen47369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47370" type="x-p"/>He does not advise Simon to tremble and hesitate in prayer; for stroh a supplication would have been vain; but he points out the heinousness of the offense; that he may strike his mind more forcibly, and may at length constrain him to rouse himself that he may approach God with true repentance. This word <hi type="italic">perhaps, </hi>therefore, does not imply doubt, but is equivalent to an expression which we commonly use, <hi type="italic">if it be possible, </hi>when we venture to hope and promise to ourselves something. And Hezekiah did not speak as if God were deaf to the words of the ungodly, or as if anything escaped his notice; but because it was a fixed principle in his heart that “God is near to all that truly call upon him,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.145.18">Psalm 145:18</reference>,) he determines to strive against despondency, and arms himself by prayer; and because he does not expect to gain the conquest without difficulty, he says, <hi type="italic">If perhaps.</hi> <note n="47"> <div sID="gen47371" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Paraventure, ou possible</foreign>.” “Perhaps, or possible.”<div eID="gen47371" type="x-p"/> </note> Besides, he mentions two kinds of hearing, which in some measure removes the difficulty.<div eID="gen47370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47372" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">If perhaps Jehovah, thy God shall hear the words which Jehovah thy God hath heard. </hi>At first sight there is some apparent contradiction in these words; but the manner of speaking is highly appropriate, because Hezekiah was assuredly and beyond all controversy convinced that nothing is hidden from God; only he argues with himself on this point, whether or not, God determines to call in question the blasphemy of this filthy dog; because frequently he delays and conceals vengeance for a time, and thus seems to shut his eyes and overlook it. In short, taking for granted that<div eID="gen47372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47373" type="x-p"/>“all things are open and manifest to God,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.4.13">Hebrews 4:13</reference>,)<div eID="gen47373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47374" type="x-p"/>he only asks with earnestness whether or not God actually shews that he is so highly offended by the blasphemies of Rabshakeh that he determines not to allow them to remain unpunished. In a word, he wishes God to hear effectually, that is, by restoring those things which were scattered and confused, and shewing himself to be a judge; for then do we know that he actually sees and observes all things. In this manner Hezekiah asks, “Hath not the Lord heard the blasphemies of Rabshakeh, to take vengeance on them, and to shew that he hath a regard to the glory of his name?”<div eID="gen47374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47375" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Jehovah thy God. </hi>By calling him “the God of Isaiah,” Hezekiah does not mean that there is only one man who worships God, nor does he exclude himself from the number of the godly; but because prayers flowed from doctrine, the pious king wished to speak in commendation of the ministry of the Prophet, and to testify that he was a true servant of God. That relation is somewhat more extensive; for all believers call on God, and, on the other hand, God reckons them among his people; but God is reckoned in a peculiar manner to be the God of Isaiah and Paul, because they have a special calling. In a word, these words expressly contain praise and commendation of Isaiah’s calling.<div eID="gen47375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47376" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Thou wilt therefore lift up a prayer. </hi>This is the second reason why Hezekiah sent messengers to Isaiah; namely, that he also would pray along with others. Hence we learn that it is the duty of a prophet, not only to comfort the afflicted by the word of the Lord, but also to offer his prayers for their salvation. Let not pastors and ministers of the word, therefore, think that they have fully discharged their duty, when they have exhorted and taught, if they do not also add prayer. This indeed is what all ought to do; but Hezekiah sent to Isaiah in a particular manner, because he ought to lead the way to others by his example. Besides, “to lift up a prayer” is nothing else than “to pray,” but the mode of expression deserves attention; for it shews how our feelings ought to be regulated when we pray. Scripture everywhere enjoins us to “lift up our hearts to heaven,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Lam.3.41">Lamentations 3:41</reference>;) for otherwise we would have no fear of God. Moreover, our stupidity is so great that we are immediately seized by gross imaginations of God; so that if he did not bid us look to heaven, we would choose rather to seek him at our feet. “To lift up a prayer,” therefore, is to pray in such a manner that our hearts may not grovel on the earth, or think anything earthly or gross about God, but may ascribe to him what is suitable to his majesty, and that our warm and earnest affections may take a lofty flight. In this sense it is said in the Psalm,<div eID="gen47376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47377" type="x-p"/>“Let my prayer come up before thee as incense, <lb/> and as the evening sacrifice.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.141.2">Psalm 141:2</reference>.)<div eID="gen47377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47378" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">For the remnant that is still left. </hi>When he desires that prayer should be offered “for the remnant of the people that was left,” this circumstance was fitted powerfully to move the Lord; not that he is moved after the manner of men, but he acts towards us in this manner, and accommodates himself to our weakness. Thus when our affairs are brought to such an extremity that we are not far from destruction, we ought to spread our misery before God, that our minds may receive some consolation; for God declares that he hath regard to “the poor and afflicted.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.22.24">Psalm 22:24</reference>.) And the nearer we appear to be to destruction, so much the more warmly and earnestly ought we to implore that he would render assistance to us, as we see here that Hezekiah did when matters were desperate.<div eID="gen47378" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.37.4" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen47365" osisID="Isa.37.4" type="section"/>
entries.27b93a068d9cc9b4f6b7896612cfcb9981ff3140: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.37.5" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.37.5" sID="gen47379" type="section"/> <div sID="gen47380" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">5.</hi><hi type="italic"> And the servants of King Hezekiah came to Isaiah. </hi>As the Prophet formerly related that the pious king had no other refuge than to consult the mouth of the Lord, so he now shews that he did not consult in vain; for he received the consolation which he desired. Instructed by this example, if we seek relief from him by pouring our cares and anxieties into the bosom of God, our hope shall never be disappointed; and although there will not always be prophets in the world, such as Isaiah was, yet he will come forth seasonably to render assistance in an appropriate manner.<div eID="gen47380" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.37.5" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen47379" osisID="Isa.37.5" type="section"/>
entries.0b4c4d9ae9f55a843e617a94686da487dba0be0d: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.37.6" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.37.6" sID="gen47381" type="section"/> <div sID="gen47382" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">6.</hi><hi type="italic"> Thus saith Jehovah. </hi>Isaiah begins by saying that he gives the reply in the name of God, and expressly declares that the oracle comes from God, both because prophets ought always to beware of bringing forward anything of their own, and because in so difficult a matter the authority of God was needful. In this manner also, the Prophet shewed that he met the prayers of the pious king. Even false prophets, indeed, boast of the name of God, but falsely. Isaiah was truly the organ of the Holy Spirit, and therefore he has a right to mention the holy name of Him that sent him.<div eID="gen47382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47383" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Fear not. </hi>When he bids him “not fear,” he exhorts Hezekiah to be of a courageous or, at least, a calm disposition. Whenever we hear this word, let us be reminded that we are enjoined to cultivate that peace which faith produces in our hearts; for all who trust in God, and expect from him deliverance from their distresses, rise superior to all fears by the exercise of patience, so that even in the midst of affliction they have peace. Besides, in order that the pious king may continue cheerfully to expect a joyful issue, he plainly declares that God conducts his own cause which he has undertaken to defend, because he cannot permit wicked men unpunished to dishonor his name without making it appear at length that he is a righteous judge. <note n="48"> <div sID="gen47384" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">En les punissant</foreign>.” “By punishing them.”<div eID="gen47384" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen47383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47385" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The servants of the king of Assyria. </hi>By calling them <hi type="italic">servants, </hi>he presents in a stronger light the baseness of the action; for although the king himself had spoken in this manner, still it would have been intolerable that the Lord should be despised and so shamefully attacked by a mortal man. Hence it might easily be concluded that much less would he endure to be so highly insulted by “servants,” <note n="49"> <div sID="gen47386" type="x-p"/> “The word translated <hi type="italic">servants, </hi>is not the same with that in the preceding verse, but strictly means young men or boys, and is so translated in the <hi type="italic">Targ. </hi>and <hi type="italic">Vulg. </hi>Many interpreters regard it as a contemptuous description, and it is so translated by Hitzig, <hi type="italic">(</hi><foreign xml:lang="de"><hi type="italic">knappen</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">, </hi>attendants.) Umbreit, <hi type="italic">(</hi><foreign xml:lang="de"><hi type="italic">buben</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">, </hi>boys or lads,) Henderson, (striplings,) and in other modern versions.” — <hi type="italic">Alexander.</hi><div eID="gen47386" type="x-p"/> </note> and therefore the rank of the person increases the heinoushess of the attack.<div eID="gen47385" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.37.6" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen47381" osisID="Isa.37.6" type="section"/>
entries.d454e6da4f70e0a3ad58625eed454cfc36003071: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.37.7" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.37.7" sID="gen47387" type="section"/> <div sID="gen47388" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">7.</hi><hi type="italic"> Behold, I will bring a wind upon him. </hi>Others translate it, “I will put my Spirit in him,” as if the Prophet were speaking of a secret influence of the heart; but that is a forced interpretation. It is a highly appropriate metaphor that there is in the hand of God a wind or whirlwind to drive Sennacherib in another direction. To compare wicked men to “straw or chaff,’ (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.1.4">Psalm 1:4</reference>) is a mode of expression frequently employed in Scripture, because God easily drives them wherever he thinks proper, when they think that they are standing very firm. The commotion that arose in the kingdom of Sennacherib is compared by the Prophet to a “wind” or “storm” which drove him out of Judea, and then he shews that the Lord will find no more difficulty in repelling that enemy than if he wished to move straw or chaff; and the very same thing might be said of all tyrants, however powerful.<div eID="gen47388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47389" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">For he shall hear a report. </hi>The words “and he shall hear” are evidently added for the sake of explanation, and therefore I have chosen to interpret them as assigning a reason, “For he shall hear.” <note n="50"> <div sID="gen47390" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="el">ἀκούσας ἀγγελίαν</foreign><hi type="italic">, </hi>“having heard a message.” “<foreign xml:lang="it">Havendo inteso un certo grido</foreign>,” “having heard a certain noise.” — <hi type="italic">Ital. </hi>“<foreign xml:lang="de">Uno foll etmas heren</foreign>,” “and shall hear something.” — <hi type="italic">Luth. Germ.</hi><div eID="gen47390" type="x-p"/> </note> This is the wind by the raising of which Sennacherib was suddenly driven away; for a report which he heard about the kings of Egypt and Ethiopia constrained him to return to his own country.<div eID="gen47389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47391" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And I will cause him to fall by the sword in his own land. </hi>This means as if he had said, “He now annoys and harasses others, and endeavors to extend widely the limits of his empire; but I will raise up enemies to him, in the very bosom of his own land, who shall discomfit him.” Some expound it to mean the land of Israel, but that is an excessively forced interpretation; for he speaks of the land of the king of Assyria himself, and there is an implied contrast, “He who subdued other men’s cities and kingdoms shall not be able to defend his own country, but shall be destroyed and perish in it.”<div eID="gen47391" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.37.7" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen47387" osisID="Isa.37.7" type="section"/>
entries.86171dd6d16cb14e246969548eb9dd5b412f1253: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.37.8" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.37.8" sID="gen47392" type="section"/> <div sID="gen47393" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">8.</hi><hi type="italic"> And Rabshakeh having returned. </hi>He now declares how Rabshakeh, without doing anything, returned to his king, not to the same place where he had left him; for he understood that he had raised the siege of Lachish, and had departed into Egypt for the purpose of attacking Libnah. Some think that this city is Pelusium, others choose rather to assign it to Judea. It is, indeed, probable that, in consequence of a report that reached him about the approach of enemies, he moved his camp towards Egypt, that by meeting them he might prevent them from advancing. Though God restrained the violence of the tyrant by a new war, in order to give some relief to the Jews, yet he did not wish to conquer the tyrant by the hand of man, but only to shew openly and, as it were, to display on a theater his unconquerable pride; because, even when he was in great danger, he did not cease to vomit out the same blasphemies, as we shall soon see.<div eID="gen47393" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.37.8" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen47392" osisID="Isa.37.8" type="section"/>
entries.401dc9bdf5985daed29c70d0c461fcec7808fa48: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.37.9" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.37.9" sID="gen47394" type="section"/> <div sID="gen47395" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">9.</hi><hi type="italic"> And hearing concerning Tirhakah king of Ethiopia. </hi>From what follows we may conjecture the reason why the king of Assyria suddenly departed from Judea; for the kings of Egypt and Ethiopia had formed a league with each other against Sennacherib, because they saw that his power was becoming excessive, and that his invasion of other countries had no limit, and therefore they readily concluded that, unless they opposed his violence at an early period, they also would be in imminent danger from him. These kings did not intend to provide for the safety of Judea at their own loss, but looked to themselves; for so great power possessed by one individual is commonly and deservedly viewed with suspicion by other princes and nations. They therefore act wisely in joining their forces and meeting him early; for separately they would easily have been subdued and destroyed.
